speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: CLOSING OF TRAINING CENTRE AT UNIVERSITY OF BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
I wish to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and I apologize for not sending him notice of it. The matter came to my attention just before coming into the house and is based on a Canadian Press dispatch from the United Nations which states: 26207-1-23
Inquiries of the Ministry
Because of heavy commitments, the United Nations has been forced to cancel financial support of the University of British Columbia's U.N. training centre, it was announced today.
The U.B.C. authorities have issued a statement to the effect that the centre will be closed on May 31 unless a satisfactory financial arrangement can be evolved. Can the minister inform the house what consideration the government is giving toward maintaining this very useful training centre?

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CLOSING OF TRAINING CENTRE AT UNIVERSITY OF BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
The United Nations regional training centre at the University of British Columbia was established in July, 1960, by the United Nations technical assistance administration. The centre itself does not conduct training programs, but it has assisted in arranging programs and in looking after the administrative arrangements for trainees sent to establishments on the west coast of Canada or in the northwestern United States. The total number of United Nations trainees handled by the centre in 1961 was 10. The centre has also been helpful in recruiting Canadians for service abroad under technical assistance programs.
In the last full year for which figures are available the United Nations contributed approximately $30,000 to the operating costs of the centre. The Canadian government has been making a grant of $10,000 annually since the fiscal year 1959-60 toward the expenses of the centre. The University of British Columbia has provided secretarial assistance, office supplies and other services which they have valued at approximately $6,000.
It is my understanding that the United Nations bureau of technical assistance operations has come to the conclusion that it is not in a position to continue direct financial support of the centre after May, 1962. The United Nations is, however, prepared to examine the possibility of making use of such a centre at the University of British Columbia on the basis of a fee for services rendered.
I am informed that the board of governors of the university have reviewed the matter in the light of this new development and apparently feel that for budgetary reasons they cannot continue the centre after May 31, 1962.
The Canadian government was prepared to continue its grant of $10,000 toward the cost of this centre. If, however, the United Nations is withdrawing its financial support and the centre is likely to be disbanded, a further grant from the Canadian government will obviously not be required.
I have gone into this matter very carefully because the University of British Columbia

Inquiries of the Ministry happens to be in my constituency, but unfortunately there was no way in which this centre could be carried on.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Transport. In view of the fact that it is the function of the Canadian maritime commission to receive applications for subsidies and to rule on these applications according to the regulations governing subsidies, will the minister advise the house whether the action of Mr. Alec Watson, chairman of the maritime commission, in sending a telegram to an agency of the B.C. government threatening loss of subsidy unless this agency followed Mr. Watson's choice of engines means that in the future the chairman of the maritime commission will direct the purchasing policy of shipbuilders and ship owners?

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have this opportunity to clear up this misunderstanding. I think it would be appropriate for me to state the facts as they have occurred.
As the house knows, under the present subsidy policy of our government a ship owner lodges an application with the maritime commission and the commission considers the application before deciding what amount of subsidy the applicant should receive. In this case concerning the government of British Columbia and the contract for the building of two new ferry boats, the president of the B.C. transport commission got in touch with the maritime commission and asked for information in advance on the possibility of subsidies for these two ferry boats. Discussion has been going on for some time between the maritime commission and the gentleman in question. A few days ago

Inquiries of the Ministry the president of the British Columbia transportation commission sent a telegram to the chairman of the maritime commission asking whether, if the British Columbia government was putting Canadian engines in these two ferries, they would qualify for the subsidy. He also sought some assurance that if the engines were of foreign manufacture-in this case, two British engines-the project would also be able to qualify.
The chairman of the maritime commission said there was no doubt, on account of the fact that these ships were being built in Canada with Canadian labour, that if the cost of engines made in Canada were added, the application would qualify for a subsidy as far as Canadian content was concerned. If, however, foreign made engines were put into these ships it would be necessary for the applicant to put in his application before he could receive an assurance that such a subsidy would be paid.
That is the situation. There is absolutely no intention of excluding other types of engines. It is simply that the Canadian maritime commission cannot say in advance of an application whether a subsidy can be paid and this is because of circumstances which hon. members will readily understand. For example, a prospective owner might use Japanese steel or German engines and so forth; we could not say in advance if the percentage of Canadian content in the case of such a ship would be sufficiently high to justify a subsidy. That is the reason for the telegram.
May I ask a supplementary question. Is it not a fact that the shipbuilding subsidy was designed to influence private builders into using Canadian shipbuilding facilities-

If so, I wonder if the Prime Minister would inform the house whether he is contemplating any action to correct the situation.
Can the Prime Minister answer today?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN CHARGES ON IRON ORE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a letter was received in my office on the 27th of this month. It is dated the 25th of January and was sent by the organization in question. As the hon. member knows, there is provision under the law regarding the course to be taken whenever objections to freight rate increases are raised. I would suggest that whatever representations are to be made should be made in the regular course to the board of transport commissioners.
I looked into the matter following the question asked by the hon. member yesterday, and the information I have received from the minister who reports for Canadian National Railways is as follows. In January, 1954 the railway company agreed to publish a rate of $1.20 per gross ton to be effective with the opening of navigation. This rate represented a reduction of 27 cents in the then effective rate. Similarly, a handling charge of 15 cents per gross ton was adopted. Both rates were to be subject to adjustments upward or downward to the same extent as variations were made in the rate from the Mesabi range to Duluth-Superior. Under this formula the rail rate as of April 30, 1961, was $1.45 and the dock handling charge 19 cents.
In agreeing to these rates it was anticipated, according to the railway company, that shipments would attain the estimates made by Steep Rock Iron Mines and later by Inland (Caland Ore Company). During the seven year period the actual tonnage shipped from the whole area has been less than 50 per cent of the estimate given in 1954, and in view of this continuing trend the railway company found it necessary to increase the rail rate and dock handling charge by 33 cents per gross ton or approximately 20 per cent. It is estimated by the railway company that the new rates at the present level of tonnage will not give more than a modest rate of return.
The interested shippers were advised of the decision to file a tariff of increased charges to become effective on May 1. Since that time several meetings have been held with interested shippers by the company to consider representations as to the effect of the increased transportation charges on their operation. I am also informed that further discussions are anticipated on a possible formula

for arriving at a rate which would benefit shippers as the total tonnage of ore from the area increases.

611. Payments to western grain producers to be distributed on the following basis, namely, $1 per cultivated acre up to a maximum of 200 acres per farm in accordance with regulations of the governor in council, $42,000,000.

Mr. Chairman, at the adjournment of the house last evening I was commenting on the sales of wheat that the Minister of Agriculture has been instrumental in negotiating, and I am sure we are all hoping that these countries will expand their demands and place further orders for grain. This has considerably relieved the pressure on the whole agricultural industry of Canada.
Production of livestock, dairy and poultry products has increased substantially in western Canada due mainly to large quantities of storage grain. This trend may result in surplus production and further stockpiling of these products. We are all hopeful of increased demands from export markets. However, conditions over which we have no control may reduce the export of grain from Canada. I am wondering if we should not now be looking forward to studying long term policies for disposing of our grain surplus. I am wondering if study should not be made to ascertain whether or not it would be good business to continue exporting our feed or cattle to the United States, in view of the fact that the finished product is often marketed in Canada. It is becoming more difficult for eastern feeders to obtain cattle in western Canada, and this may result in a further reduction in the consumption of western grain.
I favour a long term policy of the two price system for western wheat growers, because this would give them the kind of security to which they are justly entitled. I should like also to suggest to the minister that ways and means be provided for a delegation of members of the agriculture committee to study the policies other countries have adopted in taking care of their surpluses. I have always been concerned to find that these countries are able to purchase grain from Canada yet, under a subsidized
Supply-Agriculture
agricultural program, have been able to undersell us in many of the importing countries.
The people in the agricultural industry are very grateful for the leadership that this government and the minister have been giving, and are looking forward with confidence in the hope that agriculture may receive its fair share of the national income. A comparison with other countries shows that in Great Britain, where 5 per cent of the population are engaged in agriculture, they receive 5 per cent of the national income; in Denmark, where 20 per cent of the population are in agriculture they receive 18 per cent of the national income; in Canada, where 13 per cent of the population are engaged in agriculture, they receive 7 per cent of the national income.
In closing my remarks I should like to say that this is one of the reasons we are in favour of these acreage payments to subsidize western wheat producers; in other words, this measure will help them obtain a fair share of the national income. I would say that the purpose of this subsidization of agriculture has been to compensate the producers for this disparity of income in comparison with the rest of the people of Canada.

In the riding which I represent in this house, most of the farmers have been unable to harvest their grain on account of a very rainy season. This government, who speaks so much of assistance to agriculture, could have convinced the Ontario government, who holds the same political ideas, to take advantage of the Crop Insurance Act. speechtext: Shall the item carry?

Before the item carries I think we should have an explanation from the Acting Minister of Agriculture as to why no provision is being made at this time for the 1960-1961 permit book year. In other words, why has one year been missed?
The acting minister, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture have said this is a policy in lieu of the two price system for wheat grown for domestic consumption. One could argue that this measure is a strange way to bring that about, but that is not the point I want to make. If it was proper in 1958-59 to pay $1 an acre in lieu of a two

price system, and this was done in other years also, I should like an explanation from the minister as to whether, in his opinion, there were any different circumstances prevailing in the year that was missed.
I am sure this vote will get the unanimous approval and support of the house, but I am equally certain that should the government bring in another item providing double the amount of money on an acreage basis, so that we could pay for the year that is missing, it would also get the unanimous approval of the house. Can the minister explain why no provision is made for the year 1960-61?
There is no question of years being missed or not being missed. An acreage payment was made in 1958, one was made in 1960, and another one is being made at the present time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

The minister has once again underlined the fact that this is not an annual payment. I say, Mr. Chairman, it is another example of the slipshod method of carrying out business so often demonstrated by the present government, what can be described as a hit or miss method or, in the words of the president of the Manitoba farm union, "a hopscotch policy". No one can have any confidence in a government that does not have a policy, and this government does not have a policy on acreage payments.
The Prime Minister is interested in the coming election. He is concerned about votes, but he repudiates the agricultural organizations of western Canada by failing to introduce a consistent policy. I challenge the government to put this estimate in legislative form. I challenge them to make this a policy recorded in the statutes of the country, instead of making it a political matter. At the moment there is no regular basis for it, and the measure is introduced purely and simply on a political basis designed, as the Prime Minister hopes, to gather support in western Canada.
I suggest that although the Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture feel this kind of political activity and political management of the country is the way to get votes, it would be better if they would bring about a regularized system of dealing with this kind of payment and manage the country in an open way, instead of in a political roundabout, catch as catch can, pay some years and miss some others method, thus leaving the whole question in a state of confusion.
The longer you talk the more you lose.

Although we have heard that some members oppose the vote, I am quite 26207-1-24
Supply-Agriculture
sure the item will pass unanimously. It is interesting to recall that when a vote was taken in 1958, that measure was then passed unanimously. The same thing happened in 1960, and I believe it will be passed unanimously once again this year. Should the government have any doubt about the question let them call a recorded vote and find out for themselves. No one is opposed to the measure. All that some of us are saying is that the government should put it on a regular basis in legislative form and not pretend it is in lieu of a two price system.
In the main, the reason for it being introduced is because of the uncertainty of the Prime Minister so far as his fortunes are concerned in the next few months. If that were not the case, why not bring in a vote to cover the year that has been missed? Why turn down the demands made by western organizations for payment for last year?
I have another question for the acting minister, although I think I know the answer to it. I hope I may be proven wrong, but it has to do with a sentence in the speech from the throne which has been placed on the record a number of times. It stated:
The drought in the prairie provinces during 1961 has resulted in severe losses, however, and you will be asked to provide assistance by means of acreage payments to the farmers who have been affected.
I hope the government do not claim the item now being discussed is the fulfillment of that forecast in the speech from the throne. It is nothing of the kind. As the minister well knows, this item has nothing to do with drought. The money it provides will go to men who produced no grain whatsoever, and to those who produced only forage crops. Producers like that will get the $200 payment provided they have permit books. Payment will also be made to men with 1,000 acres who have had bumper crops, although there are not many in that category. The payment is not based, as is the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, on drought and adverse yields.
The government have made it clear that they do not have information as to which farmers had crop failures, but to refute that is the fact that such information is in the possession of the department. Prairie farm assistance has been paid out over a wide area in western Canada. The level of such payments was increased in 1955. The administration of that act is doing a lot of good and the government do have records in their possession as to what farmers had crop failures. Inspections have been made, the information is there, and I suggest that to carry out the statement in the speech from the throne will

Supply-Agriculture
require legislation to bring about supplementary benefits, additional benefits, designed to help those farmers who have had a crop failure.
This additional benefit has been asked of the government by farm organizations. The provision we have now is paid to everyone. It is paid to those who had no crops; it is paid to those who had good crops, and it is paid to some farmers in particular areas who are not in the business of marketing grain in any way at all.
Therefore I suggest to the minister that to carry out the forecast in the speech from the throne will require further legislation to supplement payments under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.

Mr. Chairman, such is the suspiciousness of mind and the complete preoccupation with political considerations of the hon. member for Assiniboia that he imputes nothing else, as a result, to people on this side of the chamber, and quite incorrectly so. He has stated in effect that this acreage payment is being made for purely political reasons and has implied that it is being done because, as everyone knows, we are getting on toward the end of this parliament.
This is not the situation, as is demonstrated by the fact that the payment was first made in 1958, just after an election had taken place-and not before one-and again in 1960. I think this is sufficient proof in itself that this type of assistance for western farmers, particularly the smaller farmers, is a matter of help because of a lack of income which has existed on the part of these farmers for many years past. It is not, as the hon. member for Assiniboia is trying to maintain and as certain hon. members of the official opposition are also trying to maintain, a political manoeuvre.
Then why did you not pay it last year?

If this were being paid for the first time this year they might have some cause to voice suspicions of that kind but, as I say, the first of these payments was made in 1958, the next in 1960 and the third one will be made under this measure. I think that alone demonstrates the fact that contentions and suspicions of that sort have no foundation in fact.
The hon. member for Assiniboia, on I think three or four occasions now-because as usual he has been very repetitive in this debate-has referred to the exact wording of the paragraph in the speech from the throne which indicated that acreage payments were going to be made. The

hon. member has been indulging in a good deal of semantics really, a play on words in connection with that particular paragraph. I think if it was not clear to him, it was clear to practically everybody else what was meant by that paragraph, and that this acreage payment was property predicted in it and is now before the committee for consideration.
As I stated when I first spoke in introducing this estimate on Friday last, there were several considerations in mind concerning the making of this payment. One of them was the general drought situation in western Canada, which of course caused a general decrease in income as far as farmers as a whole in western Canada are concerned. There is always the odd exception in any case concerning a large number of people or a large volume of goods or large acreages. There were a few people in western Canada who did have good crops.
Does the minister know what proportion?

A very small number had good crops last year. The general situation is that as far as the farmers in western Canada as a whole are concerned, they are going to be short of income because of the fact that their crops were about 50 per cent less than they had been on the average in the previous five years. As far as the people who had no crop are concerned, as the hon. member well knows and as I have indicated in this debate on two or three occasions, they are looked after by Prairie Farm Assistance Act payments.
That is not enough.
The hon. member always says "That is not enough".
It is not nearly enough. You have not increased it.

Mr. Chairman, in the 17 years I have been in this chamber, and the hon. member has been here for the same length of time-as it happens we both came to this house together in 1945-I have never heard any single measure introduced in this chamber with regard to which the hon. member for Assiniboia did not say "That is not enough".
That is a compliment.

He has said that, or
"peanuts", or something along this line.
That is a real compliment.

As a matter of fact you could bring in a measure to make the most impossible sort of payment in the world and the hon. member would still say it was not enough. In other words, that is his constant

plea which runs like a groove in a record in his head. No matter what happens, all he can do is put the needle down in that groove and say "It is not enough, it is not enough".
You cannot turn the record off.
Why did you not pay them for the year you missed, instead of all this abuse?
It does not matter what type of measure it is, you will get the same story from the hon. member for Assiniboia. He has now repeated it so often that nobody pays any attention to it.

What about you?

It has ceased to have any significance whatever. Then of course he went on in the general way that is usual with hon. members of the Liberal party and made a lot of gloomy predictions in connection with this program. The item shall not pass until the shocking misrepresentations to which we have just listened have been dealt with. Let us start with one. Who was in office when we first sold these exports to communist countries? The Liberal party. That is fact number one. Who objected to it when that was done? The members of the Union Nationale, the friends of the Secretary of State who is now boasting about these things. That is fact number two.

The hon. member knows that I am where I always was. I never thought these arguments of the Union Nationale about the sale of wheat to communist countries were sound. I do not think so now. But the hon. member and his friends seem to have been converted.

While Duplessis earmarks hundreds of millions for agriculture... Mr. Lapalme and his Liberal friends in Ottawa, who are more concerned about the situation in the Middle and the Far East than about the problems of the Quebec farmers, give $4,198,293,000 to foreigners-

That is the position.

It was not a sale; it was a gift.
[The Chairman.]

One hon. member says it was not a sale, it was a gift. Let me read what Mr. Duplessis had to say on this subject, not what the hon. gentleman says he said: (Translation):
The greater part of that amount in pure gifts and the rest in loans which are seldom repaid- (Text):
That latter part represents exactly what this government is doing. This government is extending credits, in other words making loans, in order that this wheat may be bought. But the difference between what the St. Laurent government did and what this government is doing is this. The St. Laurent government, when it sold wheat on credit, laid the contracts on the table so that everybody could read them. The Minister of Agriculture, together with those who support him, has refused to have this contract laid on the table. What is so secret about this? Why have so many suspicions been aroused? They exist because they have been created by hon. gentlemen opposite by their furtive, secretive tactics with regard to this contract.
I will tell hon. members the reason the minister and his supporters are so secretive about it. That contract had been signed and that wheat had been sold before the Minister of Agriculture ever went to Hong Kong. The transaction was completed by the wheat board. After it was made the minister went over there to get the credit. They do not want us to know the facts. They do not want those two dates to be compared. That is one reason we cannot see that contract in this parliament. But it is only one reason. There is another. They do not want us to see what the terms are.
What has this to do with the question before us?

If the hon. gentleman still says I am misrepresenting the situation, let him put the document on the table and let us see what the facts really are.
This government, whose leader went all over the country talking about government in secret, government by order in council and contempt of parliament, must bear responsibility for what has happened. In the whole history of this country there never has been contempt of parliament comparable with that which we have seen since the right hon. gentleman went over there to the treasury benches. This is a perfect example of the way in which the public business is treated as the private business of the Tory party.

I do not wish to prolong this debate, but I should like to associate myself and my constituents with those hon. members who have thanked the government for its work in this matter of acreage payments.

Just to give the committee an idea of how this will affect some of the small farmers in the west I should like to quote from a letter I have received from Mr. E. J. Otto, a farmer in Glenmoor, Manitoba. He says in part:
In our own case we are not quite eligible for P.F.A. yet we have had to and must still buy feed, so acreage payments would be most welcome and we would thank the government sincerely if they came through.
That is the attitude, and I may say it is the attitude of the farmers whether they support this party or the opposition. It is also significant that this measure is receiving the unanimous support of the opposition. My only disappointment is that they seem to be giving this support somewhat grudgingly; I do not feel they like to give credit to this government for anything constructive that it ever does.
We have heard speeches from members of the Liberal party which seem to have gone off at a tangent. That is understandable, because that party does not have a single member from the areas to which these payments would apply. There has been a lot of talk about parity prices and so forth. I should merely like to state in this connection that if the government had brought in a measure based on parity prices a most difficult situation would arise with respect to those farmers who had no crop to sell. When a crop fails, that is the time they would need help most, and this is the type of situation that the present measure is designed to remedy. The hon. member for Assiniboia has been saying that these payments should be made only to those who have suffered from drought.
On a point of order, I never made any such statement.

It is very hard to understand the hon. member for Assiniboia, because he leads us into such a morass that I took it from his remarks, which I read carefully, that he was trying to suggest that there are farmers who will get the payment and who will not need it.
That is true.

My understanding is that
P.F.A.A. does cover this situation and that the present measure provides for a supplementary payment which will help those who suffered from the drought. We must remember that those who did reap some harvest or who are in diversified farming also need assistance. In my own area of mixed farms this assistance is most welcome. In Springfield only 52 per cent of the grain produced is sold. The rest is used for feed and seed. Sometimes, indeed, we have to buy feed. Therefore, if we had introduced a measure based on the
Supply-Agriculture
price of wheat the benefit would not really have been as great as it is under a scheme of acreage payments.
I have the figures here to demonstrate this contention, but the argument is somewhat extraneous and I shall not go into it at this time because, as I said, I do not wish to prolong the debate. I merely wish to compliment the government on ironing out some of the difficulties which were experienced by a number of farmers when the two previous acreage payments were being made. Those of us who represent rural areas should not now be faced with problems from farmers who did not have their wheat permits or were experiencing difficulty in qualifying for these payments. This measure is welcome by all the farmers in the west. Regardless of what the opposition may say, it is a big help and it is coming at a time when the farmers who are preparing for their spring seeding and other spring work will welcome it most heartily.
Carried.

Before the item carries I wish to ask two or three brief questions for the purpose of clarification. Last Friday, as reported at page 246 of Hansard-and I am reading from the second paragraph of the first column-the minister stated as follows:
-and it is estimated that approximately 235,000 payments will be made.
My first question is this. Is it possible for a farmer to receive more than one payment or is the number of payments the same as the number of farmers? My second question is this. How many farmers actually received payment last year, and how many of the farmers expected to receive payment this year will also receive payment under the P.F.R.A.?
No one received them last year.
I mean in 1960.
The hon. member does not mean P.F.R.A. He means P.F.A.A.
Yes, P.F.A.A.
What is the difference?

In reply to the second question as to the number of people who received payments previously, may I say that in 1958 the number was 234,162. I put these figures on record on Friday. The hon. member will find them given in Hansard. In 1960 the number was 227,710. The present estimate of the department is the one that I gave.
As to the matter of who might receive these payments and whether or not a man might receive more than one, the answer is no.

Supply-Agriculture
The maximum payment to any one individual is $200, no matter how much land he has or Whether he has two or three parcels of land. In respect of the first payment that was made, there were a few individuals who had a piece of land here and another piece of land somewhere else and who had a permit book for each one. As a result they received two cheques. When the whole thing was checked afterwards they were called upon to return the extra cheque which they had received. The scheme is based on the fact of a man receiving one payment only.
So that the number of payments is the same as the number of farmers, is it?

Not necessarily. You might have a considerable number of farmers who do not have permit books. For example, consider the ranchers who have no cultivated acreage. They would not be eligible to get permit books.

Did the minister say how many farmers who may receive payment under this acreage grant or under this acreage payment item also receive payment under the P.F.A.A.? Is it possible for a farmer to receive both payments?

Yes. As a matter of fact, a large number of farmers will receive both payments. I have not here the figures as to the number of people who have already been paid and to who it is estimated will receive P.F.A.A. payments this year. I can get those figures for the hon. member and send them to him some time in the future if he is interested in them. However, I have not them here at the moment, as this matter really has nothing to do with the item which is under discussion. Everybody who has received a P.F.A.A. payment will also, I believe, receive one of these payments.

I wish to thank the minister for the information he has given. It was the procedure in which I was interested, not the details. There is only one more question I wish to ask and it is this. Is there any sort of means test in connection with this payment, or is it paid to a farmer whether he needs it or not?
No, there is no means test at all in connection with this payment. It is paid to every person who has a permit book.
That is the only requirement?
Yes.

Just before the vote carries, I wish to say that I am sure western producers 
will be disappointed that the statement in the speech from the throne will not be more accurately fulfilled by an additional measure which would provide some benefits based on crop failures. The farm organizations have been asking for such a measure. The Acting Minister of Agriculture can say "Oh, no matter what we do, the hon. member for Assiniboia says, 'more' ". I intend to keep on saying "more" so long as I think more is justified and so long as there is some support based on good evidence that such is the case.
The farm organizations have asked for supplementary payment based on crop failure. The national farmers' union came out last fall with the demand for a supplemental payment of $5 per acre to all farmers who had a crop failure as defined in the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, namely a yield of 12 bushels an acre or less, and that this $5 per acre payment should be based on half of the farmer's cultivated acreage up to 400 acres. In other words they were asking for a supplementary payment to a maximum of $1,000 in addition to the maximum payment under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. In other words they were asking for a maximum payment of $1,800 in time of crop failure.
The government's crop insurance scheme just is not working in adequate fashion at all. It is working to some extent in Manitoba. It has very limited application in Saskatchewan. The provincial government of Alberta so far has not seen fit to come into the scheme Under these circumstances I call on the government to take action to provide supplementary benefits to farmers who have suffered a crop failure and, by doing so, to fulfil the forecast in the speech from the throne.
