Special-
612. Contribution towards a special Newfoundland works program for fishing settlements that experienced income reduction resulting from decreased catches, $300,000.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall item 612 carry?
Is the minister going to make a statement?

Yes, Mr. Chairman. I intend to make a short statement in explanation of this vote.
As indicated in the wording of vote 612, this special work program in Newfoundland arose because the traditional method of inshore fishing was not fully effective in the

past year. Over a widespread area of the coast, fishermen are dependant on the use of trap nets. This is a very successful method when the cod come close to shore. This year, for some unknown reason, the cod failed to follow their usual habits. Inshore fishermen were not in a position to go far out to sea to follow the fish, so their catch was substantially reduced.
This situation began to be apparent in the statistics for June and July, and in August a formal request for assistance was received from the fishermen's organization, namely the Newfoundland federation of fishermen, emphasizing their desire for a works program.
I think the fishermen's attitude should be commended in that what they were desirous of obtaining was a works program. These fishermen are a self-reliant, industrious group of people, and we were impressed with their request. As soon as the situation became clear, discussions were arranged in St. John's by officials of the federal Department of Fisheries with officials of the fishermen's federation and officials of the provincial government. This was followed by negotiations between the two governments through which agreement was reached to proceed with a twofold program of local work projects based on (1) taking maximum advantage of the municipal winter works incentive program which had been extended to include unorganized settlements for the first time and (2) special work projects in those fishing settlements where the fishermen had been unable to secure their normal production.
The joint federal-provincial program which has been undertaken will result in some $80,000 in additional work in fishing settlements under the regular municipal winter works incentive program and approximately $350,000 of work under the special program, the federal share of which is covered by this particular vote. The figure of $350,000 includes an estimated $50,000 to be contributed by the government of Newfoundland, which agreed to meet 25 per cent of the labour cost of this special program.
Under this program special work projects have been or are being carried out in 415 fishing settlements on the east and southeast coasts of the province and in southern Labrador. Some 12,000 fishermen live in these settlements. The total expenditure of approximately $430,000 makes up for over one third of the decrease in income from fishing compared with 1960.
Responsibility for local administration of the program has been assumed by the provincial government. Reports coming to me indicate that a wide variety of local projects
Supply-Fisheries
ranging from road extensions to improvements to slipways for small fishing vessels have been going forward.
If the committee is interested, I might give two or three examples. For instance, at Bonavista there is an item of $4,925 for the preparation of a public playground for children and repair of the road to Cape Bonavista lighthouse which is an attraction for tourists. At Grate's Cove there is an amount of $3,150 for the building of roads to the public slipway and the repair and ditching of roads throughout the community. There is an amount of $4,550 at Petty Harbour for the widening and repair of roads throughout the general area and the erection of guard rails and retaining walls along the Yellow river. At Seldom and Little Seldom there is an item of $4,200 for the reconditioning of local roads and the construction of a new road to tie in a number of new settlements. At Fogo there is an item of $5,425 for repairing and widening of local roads and the filling in of a creek near the ocean which has been used as a disposal area for garbage and sewage. The latter project is being done at the suggestion of the medical health officer. At Change Islands there is an amount of $4,270 for brush cutting for a snowmobile road.
I could give other examples, but I do not think it is necessary for me to take up any more of the time of the committee. However, if the debate goes on for several days, as it did on the previous item, I should like to say that I will demand the right to hold forth perhaps at considerable length on several occasions.

Mr. Chairman, just before the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo begins, in view of the geographical distribution of the house I wonder whether the Minister of Fisheries would mind moving somewhere nearer the middle of the house for the benefit of those of us who are slightly hard of hearing.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to put a few questions to the minister arising out of the statement he has just made. If I understood the minister correctly, he said that the present winter works program which is being carried out, and for which this item is intended to provide the necessary funds, is being carried out at the suggestion of the Newfoundland federation of fishermen. It was not my understanding that the federation of fishermen requested this particular kind of program. I thought what they had in mind was a marine works program. I wish to ask the minister whether any consideration was given to substituting a marine works program for the present roads program,
3B4

Supply-Fisheries
or even including it in the present works program, and for what reason that was not done. Second, is the program that is now being carried out related in any way to the report which the minister received from Mr. Ian McArthur of the Department of Fisheries, who was sent to Newfoundland to make a survey of the particular needs of the fishermen of our province? I should like to know what recommendations, if any, Mr. McArthur made.

To answer the last question first, if I may, this item and the program are based almost entirely on the suggestions that were made by Mr. McArthur and the officials of the provincial government and others in Newfoundland with whom he had discussions. All things considered, it was felt by the officials and the government that this program would most nearly meet the problem.
There are a number of marine works projects going on under the regular program of the Department of Public Works which are in addition to this provision, of course, but such programs as marine works are fairly large items. The hon. member is far more fully aware than I am of the difficulties involved in trying to make work available to people who are spread along a great coast line, and these larger projects are carried out in isolated places. We were trying to find a program which would have application almost everywhere, because naturally there was little relationship between the catch in any particular area and what works programs could be effectively carried out there. The catch was down in areas where there are already new wharves and in some cases where we have built community stages. It would not be feasible, of course, to build another stage or anything else that was not needed in that area. We were trying to find a plan that would have wide application and would be beneficial.
It has been suggested that wharves and larger projects would be more suitable, but the difficulty is that these large projects would have the effect of providing a very desirable amount of employment in one particular area where they were being built, but they would provide no benefit at all for fishermen who were some distance away from them. We are trying to evolve a program with a much wider application.

I think the minister misunderstood the main point of my question. I quite understand that you cannot build wharves everywhere. If a community already has a wharf you do not build another just to make work for somebody. This is not what I had in mind. What I had in mind, and I thought

I stated it clearly, was this. Why not include that type of program in this winter works scheme for communities where it can be done? This was the question I had in mind. However, marine works have been excluded even from communities where they are needed and could be usefully carried out. I should like the minister to clarify that if he can.
While I am on my feet I have a couple of more questions which perhaps I should put at this time. Was any consideration given to extending the same principle of payments to the fishermen that was incorporated in the acreage payments to farmers which we have just voted? Was any thought given to using the administrative machinery of the unemployment insurance commission to distribute the funds directly to the fishermen?

Consideration was given to the general idea that the hon. member mentions but it was found not to have practical application, because the situation of farmers and fishermen is entirely different. It is true they have many things in common. They are both primary producers of food. However, when you have said that you have gone about as far as you can go in making a valid comparison between the situation of fishermen and farmers. In the case of fishermen it is more difficult to measure the amount of effort or equipment used in attempting to catch fish than it is in the case of a farmer where the extent of a man's operation and his industry are there for all to see. I might be missing the point the hon. member has, but I must say that this situation was taken into consideration.
I neglected to answer a previous question, but the request from the federation of fishermen was for a work program, and they gave a considerable list of suggested schemes, including the types that are covered by this vote.

This principle of extending equal treatment to all Canadians, Mr. Chairman, is to me a sound one. The minister has not said anything as yet to convince me that it is impossible to extend the same principle to distressed fishermen that we have applied to relieve the needs of distressed farmers. We have in front of us today a sheet of further supplementary estimates which contains four items. The first two of these items are allocations to relieve distress. The first item, the one with which we have just dealt, is to relieve the needs of distressed farmers. The one we are discussing now is to relieve the needs of distressed fishermen. This sheet itself bears concrete evidence of the discrimination that is taking place.

I should like to deal with this discrimination under four headings. The first heading is the reason for it. The reason given by the minister on Friday, and on subsequent occasions since, for making acreage payments to farmers was to supplement their income. He did not make any reference at all to the amount of effort they put forth or anything like that. All that was required was a permit book and 200 acres of land and they could get $200. It was purely a measure to compensate for the low income which has resulted from the vagaries of nature over which the farmers had no control whatever.
Perhaps it would be worth-while to put on the record the statement the minister made on Friday in that connection. I am reading now, Mr. Chairman, from page 245 of Hansard for January 26, 1962: The minister had listed the four reasons for making acreage payments to farmers, and then he went on to say this:
This year there is a very important additional reason why a payment of this kind should be made. It is to be found in the reduced farm income, particularly of people in certain areas of western Canada due to the drought which took place there last year. This drought in the long run did not prove as devastating and serious as at one time was believed would be the case, but nevertheless it did have very serious effects which are particularly apparent in the income position of many farmers in western Canada. How serious that is can be shown by comparing the average wheat yield this year with that of previous years. During the past crop year the average wheat yield is estimated to have been 10.4 bushels per acre, whereas for the previous five years it was 19.7 bushels per acre. In other words, this year's yield was not very much more than half of what had been secured on the average in the previous five years. This gives a good indication of the situation in which many farmers will find themselves, and demonstrates the necessity of assistance in the form proposed.
Well, that is a very clear statement, Mr. Chairman, as to the reason for these payments. The need applies identically in the case of the fishermen. They are suffering from reduced income, just the same as the farmers. They have to live; they have children to feed, families to support. They have the identical needs of the farmers. In addition to that, they have to make some provision in order to be in a position to continue their occupation when the season opens.
There is one important difference in the case of the farmers. The minister stated that their income was down almost half because of the poor crop yield. In other words the crop this year is little better than half what it would be in a average year but, in the case of many fishermen, it is much worse than that because they had no crop yield at all. I know many of them in my own riding whose crop this year is only about 25 per cent of what it was last year, and it must be remembered that last year was a poor year.
Supply-Fisheries
The percentage would be less than that if we were to compare last year's yield with the average over the past five years, as was done in the case of the farmers.
Fishermen have as great a claim to aid as the farmers and I believe, when distress is to be relieved, compensation for the fishermen should be on exactly the same basis as it is for farmers. To treat fishermen differently is tantamount to discrimination. The sheet I hold in my hand gives evidence of discrimination in the form in which the assistance is to be paid. In the case of the farmers we have a very special measure of assistance, particularly designed for them, and with no strings attached.
When I am speaking on the subject I should like to point out to my hon. friends that this asistance is not the only aid being given to the farmers. It comes on top of other assistance which they can receive by way of Prairie Farm Assistance Act grants and other grants. But, so far as fishermen are concerned, there are no other payments by which their income can be supplemented. This is the only one; but when payments are made to farmers we do not include that aid in an expanded works program. We do not provide it in such a way that it would apply equally to small prairie town merchants and to labourers. The measure is applicable to farmers, and farmers only. On the other hand, in the case of fishermen the aid for them has to be fitted into some sort of winter works program, not specifically designed for fishermen and which cannot be administered in a way that will benefit fishermen alone.
The third discrimination which appears in this sheet is the amount. A farmer may receive up to a maximum of $200, in addition to other payments under other farm legislation. However, while $300,000 is provided for fishermen it is conditional upon the provincial government also making payments. The acreage payments to farmers are not conditional on anything done by the provincial governments in the prairie provinces, and I would like to know why fishermen are singled out for such treatment.
The $300,000 being made available for fishermen is contingent upon a contribution of 25 per cent of the labour content of the program being made by the government of Newfoundland, and that government must also complete the rest of the usual roads maintenance program, which will cost $80,000 from the middle of October. Thus, the federal government is providing $300,000 on condition that the provincial government puts up $80,000 and $50,000. All these conditions are attached before a fisherman can get one cent. But even when these conditions are fulfilled

Supply-Fisheries
what will he get? Our premier has worked it out at about $20 per fisherman simply because this $300,000 is not all to be spent on labour. It is for roads, bridges and some of the other things the minister mentioned this afternoon. Materials have to be bought out of that sum and so the amount a fisherman will get will perhaps be around $20, to meet the needs of his family for the whole of the winter.
There is a further, additional discrimination because when we look at the first item in the supplementary estimates we see that the government itself takes full responsibility for the administration of the payments to farmers. It states:
Payments to western grain producers to be distributed on the following basis, namely, $1 per cultivated acre up to a maximum of 200 acres per farm in accordance with regulations of the governor in council.
However, when it comes to relieving distressed fishermen the federal government takes no responsibility for the administration of the fund. It is to be administered in the best way possible. The minister pointed out the difficulties however when he said the $300,000 has to be spent in hundreds of settlements scattered around a 4,000 mile coast line. Since the government takes responsibility for administering aid to distressed farmers why can it not take the same responsibility for administering aid to distressed fishermen? Why has it refused to take that responsibility? I would like the minister to answer that question when he replies.
In his introductory speech I understood him to say that the winter works program is really the suggestion of the fishermen's federation, and that everybody in Newfoundland is in agreement with it. I am sure the government received advice from provincial authorities pointing out that such a type of winter works program is not really suitable because most of the settlements in question cannot carry out that kind of program in the winter months. It just cannot be done, and if equipment has to be used then the labour content is whittled down.
There is no administrative machinery to administer this grant. Some 575 settlements had road work done last year and I presume this item is related to the moneys already expended in those settlements. As I said already, most of these settlements are isolated and are scattered around a 4,000 mile coast line. There is no administrative machinery, yet the federal government expects somebody in the provincial government to take responsibility for administering this aid.
In addition to the difficulties of administration there is the further difficulty of discriminating between one fisherman and another as to which should receive work. In
other words, somebody in a settlement has to devise a means test in order to be able to say to one fisherman "you earned enough this summer, your catch was not too bad so you cannot get in on this program", and to another fisherman "your catch was down and you are entitled to participate." In other words, somebody has to select people in the community to work on a winter works program and refuse work to others. Not only that, but there is the difficulty of deciding borderline cases, when the fisherman is perhaps a borderline case and is in need, or perhaps a logger or labourer who has been out of work and not able to meet the needs of his family. These people need this assistance just as much as the fisherman who has had a poor catch. But the government washes its hands completely of any responsibility of administering this fund. It throws the whole problem into the lap of the provincial government, the municipal authorities, the local roads boards or whoever is willing to accept it. It does not lay down any direction for them with regard to the way this money is to be administered.
I wish to say to the minister that I am not against this item of $300,000. It is better than nothing. I suppose even $20 will buy something. However, when you break it down to a family it is only about 13 cents a day per family, or about 3 cents per head per family, and I do not know what they will get out of it. That is what it amounts to. When we contrast that with the way we help farmers, it defies words to describe the comparison.
Watch yourself.

Yes, I will watch myself. My blood pressure is getting up. Certainly the time has come when we should not discriminate between one group of Canadians and another. When we make that kind of discrimination between groups that are in distress, in my opinion it is a most shameful thing to do.

Mr. Chairman, I regret that the item before the committee has no direct application to the fishing industry on the west coast. However, because all of us in this house should concern ourselves as much as possible with matters affecting other sections of the country and the economy I should like to make one or two comments with respect to this item, even though it is far removed from my constituency and British Columbia and is in fact confined to the province of Newfoundland.
During the last couple of days we have been listening to the debate which has just concluded regarding the $1 an acre payment

to western grain farmers. In view of that debate I felt sure the Minister of Fisheries would revise his thinking and introduce an additional supplementary estimate based upon, say, $5 per foot per fishing vessel or something of that nature, in order that the assistance given from the public treasury to some of our people in the basics of farming and fishing would bear some equitability.
The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo dealt quite extensively with the theme that the item before us represents, in a number of aspects, an approach to discrimination as between fishermen and farmers. I agree with him in this regard. However, I think we must extend this concept of discrimination to types of fishermen and fishermen in different locales. I say this because certainly the salmon fishermen in British Columbia for two consecutive years, and especially two seasons ago, were disastrously hit by poor salmon runs, a poor catch and the like.
One of the worst salmon fishing seasons in the last 50 or 60 years took place two years ago on the west coast and many of the salmon fishermen there-this industry composes a large section of the economy of the province -went deeply into debt. Many of them went completely bankrupt because they just could not stand the economic situation that resulted from the poor salmon season.
We agreed to pay $1 an acre to western farmers because of drought conditions; but if drought conditions affect the salmon industry, the government tends to disregard the fact, although it is substantially the same sort of condition. Salmon fishermen were hit by drought on the coast when spawning creeks or salmon creeks dried up because of lack of rain. When this occurs the Department of Fisheries steps in and closes the season to allow for the greater escapement of spawning salmon upstream so that two or four years hence on the return we might expect a larger salmon run than would otherwise be the case if we engaged in catching a large number of salmon.
This is a deliberate action on the part of the Department of Fisheries on the west coast as a result of drought conditions that affect the income and the catch of fishermen out there. We do not see any indication of any concern, or of any approach either in the supplementary estimates before us or in any of the main estimates that I can ever recall participating in studying, for any special consideration for fishermen on the west coast of this nation. I think this is also a form of discrimination.
The herring industry on the coast was in the doldrums for a couple of years. In addition to the salmon industry, the whaling fleet has
Supply-Fisheries
been tied up as a result of several factors, and the income of the people following these particular fisheries of salmon, herring and whaling has not been too good in the past few years. I do not wish to complain too much about this because I realize it is not specifically covered by the item before us. We are concerned with contributions toward a special Newfoundland winter works program. I only mention that similar conditions existed in the province of British Columbia in other fisheries and would plead with the minister to take into account these conditions which exist on the west coast of Canada as well as those which exist on the east coast, in order that some balance and equitability may come into play in considering what assistance and help may be given from the public treasury to these primary producers.
Last session, I believe, we had some discussion about the attitude developing amongst west coast fishermen toward what relatively speaking, is considered to be an inordinately large degree of concern by the government with respect to fishermen on the east coast. We found that in the past the Fisheries Prices Support Act applied almost entirely to east coast fisheries products. To my knowledge it has never applied to the west coast. We found that there was special assistance to the Newfoundland bait service, to the east coast salt fishery, special assistance with respect to the construction of fishing boats, and the like. All this leaves the west coast fisherman, as has been explained to me, with wonderment in his mind as to whether or not he is being discriminated against. He is not complaining about the fact that this help and assistance is being given to his fellow fishermen on the east coast, but merely concerned as to whether or not this represents a form of discrimination.
I say to the minister, as did the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo, that if it is considered fair and equitable that the public treasury should assist western grain producers because of drought conditions to the extent of $1 an acre, I think it is a bit of an insult to give the fishermen in Newfoundland an amount of $300,000. It is an even greater insult to disregard entirely the salmon fishermen of the west coast who have been in equal difficulties as a result of a poor harvest of fish.

It does seem to me that there is a good deal of disparity between the treatment we have seen accorded to western farmers in the last two days of our debate and the treatment which is now accorded to the fishermen of Newfoundland.
Let me say at once that I am not objecting in any way to the assistance which has been given to western farmers under the first item. I think most people in Canada will recognize

Supply-Fisheries
that the past summer, as well as other summers of recent date, have been difficult times for farmers living in the three prairie provinces. Since these people are suppliers of food engaged in a primary industry I think it is fair in such circumstances that the federal government should help them on the grounds that their normal way of making a living has been interfered with by difficulties not of their own making. The Acting Minister of Agriculture used the argument the other day that if the western farmer were assisted during a period when his income was below normal, such assistance would eventually spread out to all parts of the country and the country would be better off in consequence of such assistance having been given. I think that is a fair argument. But if that argument is fair as applied to farmers who work in the three prairie provinces it is surely equally fair when applied to the fishermen of Newfoundland. At the moment I cannot understand the difference between the payments accorded to the fishermen of Newfoundland and those which have been accorded to the western farmers. Perhaps the minister will explain to me later where the difference lies.
Let us look at the amount themselves. I recognize that amounts and figures in themselves do not tell the whole story. Nevertheless, they have some significance. In the first place, as the minister told us the other day, about a quarter of a million farmers-not quite as many, according to the figures he used-are to be paid a total of something over $40 million, or an average of $178 per farmer. In Newfoundland, this amount of $300,000 will mean the payment of about $20 per fisherman under the present scheme. If that latter payment were accorded to the western farmers the vote which we have just approved would have amounted to approximately $5 million instead of $40 million. Let me put it in another way. The population of the three prairie provinces is approximately seven times as great as that of Newfoundland. If $300,000 is to be given to Newfoundland on a per capita basis-I am not arguing that it should be done in that way-then that sum would correspond to a little more than $2 million for the western farmer. These are just ordinary figures which do not tell the whole story but they do show the disparity between the treatment of both sides, and it is a disparity which I think the minister ought to explain.
There are other disturbing features about the plan which has been set up to aid the Newfoundland fishermen. In the first place, under the present scheme the Newfoundland fisherman has to go out and earn the amount of money he is intended to receive under this program. I have no objection to that. But as far as the western farmer is concerned, the 
money will go to him, according to the minister today, whether he is in need of it or not. The farmer concerned will receive the money because he has a permit book and because he has a certain number of acres under cultivation. True it is, according to the minister, that a number of prairie farmers had their crops reduced by 50 per cent during the past year.
May I just remind the hon. member of this: did the acting minister not say that the total crop was down by nearly 50 per cent? I have it right here.
That is right. That is what my hon. friend just said.
It is a very different thing.
A different thing from what, may I ask the hon. member for St. John's West?

A different thing from what you said. The hon. member said some were down by 50 per cent. The minister said yesterday as reported at page 314 of Hansard:
I said that drought conditions throughout the west as a whole had resulted in little more than a half crop, and that applied all throughout western Canada.

The minister's knowledge of statistics amazes me. If the average crop brought in by the western farmer is 50 per cent of the normal crop then obviously some farmers were down more than 50 per cent and some not as much as 50 per cent. When we say that the average crop was down by 50 per cent we are saying that a large number brought in a crop of far less than 50 per cent as compared with the year before. Surely, that is understandable.
That is not what you said.

If the hon. member for St. John's West will sit in his seat and allow me to say what I want to say he would find out exactly what I have in mind and what I intended to say. I am very surprised that the hon. gentleman should be standing up now trying to say something for the fishermen of Newfoundland. I hope he will.

Give me a
chance.

Another thing is this: The money paid to the western farmer is paid by cheque. The money paid to the Newfoundland fishermen has to be worked for. In addition, the money paid to the western farmer has nothing to do with the provincial government. However, as far as Newfoundland

is concerned, the province has to make a contribution, otherwise the federal government does not pay anything. One of the strings attached to the payment made to Newfoundland is that the province must make some contribution. I think this is a significant difference.
One of the most serious differences is the fact that when the money was paid to the western farmer the whole plan was administered by the federal government. I shall not deny that administering this plan with respect to the fishermen of Newfoundland may be difficult. However, it might well be difficult to administer it in respect of the western farmers.
I do not understand why the administration of this program in Newfoundland should be placed upon the shoulders of Newfoundland officials.
There are many things which could have been done in some places-not in all places- which would have produced a much greater benefit than is likely to be produced by the present scheme.
When the minister spoke a short while ago he said that much of the plan had been concentrated around the east and southeast coasts. My riding includes the northern section of St. Barbe and there we have many small settlements which even yet have no wharf or breakwater. I think the most sensible assistance which could be given to these people would be to enable them to go into the woods and cut timber so that in the spring they might build their wharf or breakwater. I recognize part of the argument used by the minister, namely that this plan would work only in some places and give work to only a few fishermen. But in many cases these are the very people who are affected by the crop failure among the fishermen of Newfoundland. I believe they could be assisted to a greater extent by some such plan. I can think of many places along the west coast where the fishermen would have benefited greatly if they had been given the opportunity to engage in some public works project rather than the one that is now recommended by the Minister of Fisheries. When the minister replies I hope he will tell us how many fishermen are concerned in this plan, according to the survey which he has made in Newfoundland; where these fishermen live or where these places are; and how the fishermen are going to be assisted as well under the plan he has proposed as they would have been assisted under a plan similar to that which has been proposed for the western farmers.

I should like to associate myself with the remarks made by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo and the hon. member for Humber-St. George's. Previously
Supply-Fisheries
I have contended-and I thought my contention was a reasonable one-that the Canadian fisherman should receive the same treatment as that received by the Canadian farmer. It seems to me to be quite obvious that such is not the case. As a matter of fact, as can be seen from the sheet which is now on our desks, a comparison between what is written under "Agriculture" and what is written under "Fisheries" would seem to point out that a great gulf exists between these two producers; I refer to the farmer who produces grain and the fisherman who produces fish. Nevertheless both are essential to the Canadian economy. Both are engaged in basic industries. Each in his respective area is equally important.
The case for the Newfoundland fisherman, or perhaps I had better say "the Canadian fisherman", in my opinion has never been given the serious consideration it deserves. There may perhaps be on the part of those in government a lack of knowledge of the real needs. Without going into the whys and wherefores, certainly the fact is-and it is more apparent today than ever before-that the Canadian fisherman is not getting the same consideration as the Canadian farmer. His problem is not looked upon in the same light. The whole concept of his needs evidently is different from that of the needs of other producers.
In connection with the works program I should like to say that I am one of those who believe that a program of marine works and a program of supplying material for fishermen, would be better than the one which has been decided upon. The minister pointed out -and quite reasonably, I would say-that large marine works such as community stages would mean a considerable amount of work in one locality and none in others, and that there would not be the same spreading of work. This objection would hardly apply if small marine works were considered and if assistance in the way of material for fishermen to repair their traps, their nets and their stages were to be supplied.
I think the minister also said that it was difficult to assess a fisherman's property compared with a farmer's property. The fisherman's property consists of his boat, his trap, his stages and his flakes. They are all very real and tangible assets which can be seen and appraised. Small works have proven to be valuable to the fisherman. I refer to things such as small wharves, small landing docks or small breakwaters. These things require no argument to support them because it has been amply demonstrated over the years that where these works are supplied fishermen can carry on their vocation much better, that the fishing season is quite frequently lengthened

Supply-Fisheries
and that the fishermen's activities are facilitated with the result that the income of the individual fisherman is increased.
If I may, I should like to mention community stages here and to say that this argument applies to them to an even greater degree. If there was one program which was wisely conceived, it was the community stage program. It has been a source of bitter disappointment to me that more of these stages are not being built at the present time.
As to fishermen's property may I say that, owing to the fact that their income was low during the past year, many fishermen will face the coming year with traps that are really unfit to use, engines that are not really serviceable and boats that badly need to be repaired, to say nothing of their stages, flakes and so on. It seems to me that if assistance were given to fishermen to purchase materials so that they could put their property in shape, they themselves supplying the labour, so that when the fishing season starts they could more efficiently prosecute the fishing, two extremely worthy objectives would be accomplished at the same time. Relief would be given to the extent that materials which they needed, and which they would not be obliged to buy, would be supplied to them thus saving their meagre cash, and production would be increased as they would face the fishing season with more adequate equipment with which to do their work.
Apart from everything else, it seems to me that a real chance has been missed to accomplish something worth while and at the same time to give relief to people who badly need it. The fact is that there are many fishermen-and I am speaking of my own riding-who this year had a very poor fishery; they suffered a real crop failure. They need the kind of assistance which would permit them to become self-sustaining, independent and, one would hope, prosperous citizens of Canada during the coming year.
I shall not repeat what the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo who spoke earlier said about a different approach or a different method of handling this relief, except to say that I agree entirely with what he said. However, I would say that the time must come when the Canadian fisherman is considered on a basis of equality with the Canadian farmer. His problems must be approached with the same attitude of mind. In the fisheries of Canada we have an industry which, although very old, is still very important and in many respects still shows amazing vitality. It is of benefit not merely to the fishermen themselves but to all of Canada. In the province of Newfoundland alone the industrial areas of Canada have a great

captive market. It is to the benefit of Canada as a whole that the fisherman be given the recognition which he deserves. In asking for that I am not asking for special consideration. All I am asking is the ordinary consideration usually accorded to Canadian producers.

Mr. Chairman, we have been listening to hon. members from Newfoundland plead the case in favour of their fishermen. Frankly, I cannot object to such a plea because the fishermen of my riding are in much the same situation. I believe that the problems of the Magdalen islands are quite similar to those in Newfoundland. The fishermen of Newfoundland catch a good run of salmon at a certain season of the year. When the cod run comes the fishing may be good for a short period of time but during recent years there has been a failure during two months of the fishing season. In my riding lobster fishing is the greatest revenue producer. However, the fishing season lasts only four to six weeks and in 1961 the season was shortened by three or four weeks because of the lateness of the arrival of spring.
However, having heard members from Newfoundland speak about their problems, I should like to refer them to the last report of the Department of Fisheries where I find the following on page 89 with respect to the Atlantic coast fisheries:
With the exception of Quebec, all Atlantic provinces registered increases in the volume of landings.
On page 90 there are these words:
Newfoundland small-boat fishermen started the summer season with record landings in May and June but by midsummer the entire situation changed and catches began to dwindle.
Where I differ from them is-
I wonder whether I could ask the hon. member what year that is?
This is 1960.
We are talking about 1961.
I believe that I heard the same plea from the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate in 1961 as in 1960.
No, it was in 1958, and I will have something further to say about that.

The solutions to the problems which have been advanced by the hon. members we have heard have involved the construction of stages, the construction of ports, wharves and so on. If we are going to have the same situation occur every year, we are soon going to run short of land on which to build wharves and these other projects. In my opinion the solution does not lie in the

construction of these projects but rather in the finding of new species of fish and the development of new methods of catching and processing the product and improving its quality.
I remember speaking on this matter last year. At that time I pointed out to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that if the weather was not favourable in Newfoundland for the drying of codfish the fish could be sent to the Gaspe peninsula where the weather was more favourable and the cod could be sold as Gaspe cured cod, which brings the best price on the market.
That would not help fishermen much who caught none this year.
May I ask the hon. member if that is a promise?

There is one thing I want to say at the outset and that is I believe every hon. member of this committee would have as his objective complete fairness and justice as between all segments of the economy of this country. Some members of

Supply-Fisheries
the committee, however, are not willing to concede that this statement applies to members on the government benches. I want to say that a fair comparison of the situation cannot be achieved by comparing things that are not comparable. You cannot arrive at any basis for a just estimate if you compare horses with rabbits and start from that premise.
First, I want to say a word about the situation so far as production is concerned. There have been comparisons made on the basis of these two items in the estimates and it was stated the Newfoundland fishermen were being discriminated against. Statements were made to the effect that this vote is an insult to the fishermen when $42 million is being provided for western farmers. I should like to point out that for the whole area covered by the acreage payments, production is down about 50 per cent. This production has an aggregate value of about $400 million, in very rough figures. The item that has been voted is about 10 per cent of that.
In the case of the Newfoundland fishery, taking it as a whole, the income of fishermen in 1961 as compared with the average for the previous three years is down 1 per cent.
What about 1960?
I am talking about 1961 as compared with the average for the previous three years.
Would the minister permit me a factual question on that? He made a comparison of the western farmers' situation between 1960 and 1961. Would he take the same two years for Newfoundland?
I am not sure that I have those statistics.
That is the comparison.
This basis would vary the deduction somewhat, but it would only be in degree. I should like to point out that-
Would the minister permit another question on that same point?
Yes.
When the minister says production-I thought he said it was down by 1 per cent-
That is the value.
It is down 1 per cent in value, but is that the total cash including fish landed by draggers? Does that figure relate only to the shore fishermen?
It is income per fisherman.
That includes all fishermen?
That is right.
Does the minister not have the figures for the shore fishermen, the ones we are supporting?

I have the figures by areas, these are statistical areas, and area A was down compared with the previous three year average by 16 per cent. I shall name these areas around the coast of Newfoundland clockwise. Area B was down 3 per cent; C was down 10 per cent; D was up 14 per cent; E was down 25 per cent; F was down 5 per cent; G was up 10 per cent; H was up 6 per cent while area I was up 23 per cent. I am now getting into Humber-St. George's, although I may still be in Burin-Burgeo. Area J was up 69 per cent; K was up 21 per cent; L was up 7 per cent; M was up 8 per cent; N was up 11 per cent and area O was down 23 per cent.
Now, in addition to that, although this has very little direct bearing on the situation from which the fishermen suffered last summer, I am happy to report and I think all hon. members would be happy to know, that at the present time fresh fish are bringing the highest price on record along the south coast of Newfoundland. Certainly, it is the highest price since union with Newfoundland. I give hon. members full credit for sticking up for their constituents and for the industry in which those constituents are engaged. I do not object to this. However, when they say, let us treat the fishermen in exactly the same way as we treat the farmers, I should like them to think of some of the things they would be forfeiting as well as some of the things they would be gaining before they take that step.
Like P.F.A.A.

Would the hon. gentleman suggest that fishermen should not be entitled to salt assistance, to unemployment insurance, to a subsidized bait service or to a subsidized vessel building program under which this government has increased the rate of assistance from $155 a ton to $250 a ton? There are no comparable things done for farmers. I am willing to admit right away that, on the other hand, there are things that are done for farmers that are not done for fishermen. It is not all one-sided.
I may have misunderstood one hon. gentleman who spoke previously, but I thought he objected to us requiring a contribution from the provincial government. I must say this contribution was not a requirement, it was a voluntary contribution. In this connection, I should like to quote what the

premier of Newfoundland said in connection with the circumstances under which this program was evolved.
Would the hon. gentleman quote the messages right from the beginning so we can have the whole sequence of events and ascertain how this came about?

This would be very involved. I am not sure I have a complete file with me. There is a thick file of correspondence, and it would take at least the rest of this day if I were to read it.
Premier Smallwood had this to say, as reported in the daily News of December 1, and this is a direct quotation:
The discussion-

referring to the discussion taking place between officials of the federal Department of Fisheries and the government of Newfoundland-
-was very thorough and exhaustive and was conducted in a spirit of cordial co-operation, all present sharing a strong desire to work out the details as quickly as possible so that the benefits of the scheme may be brought to the fishermen with the least possible delay.
He went on to say:
In connection with this extra amount of $300,000 the government of Canada have accepted the offer of the Newfoundland government, made by me a few weeks ago, to pay 25 per cent of the total labour cost of the winter works projects that are carried out with this money. A considerable number of federal marine works and other public works projects have been carried out around the coast line of Newfoundland, and some are still in course of construction, and it is hardly necessary to say these special winter works will not, for the most part, be carried out in places where these larger jobs have gone ahead or are now going ahead.
The Canadian Department of Fisheries and the Department of Labour and our own Newfoundland department of fisheries and department of highways are working closely together, in the friendliest spirit possible, to get the whole scheme working without delay so that the benefits may be felt as soon as possible.
Now my department, in perfectly good faith and trying to do the best thing possible for the fishermen in Newfoundland, and trying to evolve a program which would be just, as compared to programs that are evolved for other parts of the country, not only for other industries but for other parts of the fishing industry, has evolved this scheme.
In that connection it is interesting to note that the hon. member for Skeena, in his contribution to this debate, helped to point out how very difficult it is to be absolutely fair and to be sure that justice is done to all. He said that the fishermen in his riding consider certain things are done for fishermen on the east coast which are not done for the fishermen on the west coast and he maintained that the government is prejudiced in
Supply-Fisheries
favour of fishermen on the east coast. I do not think that is so because, comparing fishermen with farmers, when you compare fishermen on the east coast with fishermen on the west coast you have two different situations to consider. There are vast amounts of money spent for fish ladders and that sort of thing for fishermen on the west coast, to make it possible for the salmon harvest there to be continued, while moneys are not spent to the same extent on the east coast.
Having said that, I now turn to the problem of fair administration. It is fair to say that the provincial government through its municipal roads system which is already set up in all of these areas, and which functions every year, was the most reasonable avenue to reach into all these little communities. There is also the problem that there is a great variation between one little area and the next, and even between one fisherman and the next. Therefore the local people who are on the ground would be best able to say where jobs were most needed. Such people located on the coast would know the situation much better than any official from Ottawa.
A scheme was suggested by hon. members whereby needy fishermen could be given grants or material for repairing their boats, equipment, and so on. On the face of it it is a fine idea. It just sounds wonderful; but on studying it we very quickly concluded that it is one which would be absolutely impossible to administer. To arrive at any degree of justice not only would you have to have a means test for a fisherman but you would have to determine what his income was.
You did not have a means test for the acreage payments.
I admit that, but I say that if we were trying to be fair-
Then you were not with the acreage payments?

Objections were raised in some cases that acreage payments were being made to men with large acreages and good crops, but in the case of the people of Newfoundland we tried the opposite thing. We tried to place the money where it was most needed, make it available to those who needed it most, who would make the best use of it, and who thereby in many cases would qualify for unemployment insurance.
Even if it were possible to arrive at absolute justice in the administration of any scheme one would still be criticized by those who think they should have got more or who think somebody else should have got less, and that is where the problem arises. As I said, the plan suggested by some of the hon.

Supply

Fisheries
members from Newfoundland with regard to advancing grants to fishermen is, on the face of it, a good one, but it would have to be carried through in a blanket fashion to cover all fishermen whether they needed it or not.
Just as you did for the farmers.

To which you
objected.
Why not treat the fishermen as well as the farmers are treated?

Because there are so many other benefits which accrue to fishermen that do not accrue to farmers such as unemployment insurance, assistance under the fishing vessel assistance act, salt assistance, and so on. In carrying out a program of assistance of any sort the picture has to be painted with a wide brush. It is difficult to do it any other way because you would have to go back a thousand years and institute a sort of domesday book to arrive at who was entitled to so much, so that in a mathematical way you could make sure each fellow was getting exactly what he deserved in relation to his effort, his needs, his family, his bad luck, and his luck in the runs of fish and so on. It is for reasons of that sort that the acreage payment is administered on a rather arbitrary basis.
I am the first to admit that the amount involved in the case of the Newfoundland fishermen is small. It is $.3 million, $300,000, and the reason it is small is that it represents 35 per cent of the drop in income.
As has been said, if it were distributed evenly to everybody it only works out at 13 cents a day for the head of every family. The reason it works out at that figure for the head of every family is because the drop in income earned by the head of every family in Newfoundland this year, statistically on the average as compared with last year, would be three times that amount-39 cents. I think it is a week rather than a day, but those statistics do not impress me very much. What you are doing is taking the amount, then dividing it by the number of fishermen and dividing it by the number of days between then and now. In effect you are almost taking the cube root of it if you divide any figure by two other factors. Even if you take the cube root of the speed of light you come up with something that is relatively small.
I wonder if I could ask the minister a question on this point?
Yes.

Does the minister think that in making these comparisons and computations, which he says he wants to make fairly,

in contrast to those on this side of the chamber which he says have been made unfairly, it is fair to include the landing from draggers with the shore fishery?
No one is suggesting that the dragger fishermen should be included in any scheme at all. It seems to me that if the minister would take the shore fishery, which is the only comparable thing, he would get a very different picture. I think the minister knows that.

Yes, but not such a very different picture, because even in the case of the shore fishery there were large areas in Newfoundland where the catch was up as compared with last year. But I would agree that if you take a small enough unit there are little communities-or if you get down to one boat, one crew-which perhaps caught no fish last year. However, it is difficult to fit them into a program that is supposed to apply to the whole of Newfoundland, unless you try to do it in the very way which has been suggested and which the provincial government agreed to undertake in the first instance.
Apparently this scheme suddenly became very unpopular, with the provincial government after they had agreed to it and had thought it was a fiine idea.
On that point, Mr. Chairman, could I ask the minister if he would read the document in which the provincial government agreed to this scheme?
I am not sure that I have that document available, but we can get it.
Perhaps the minister could get it by nine o'clock.

I think so. Probably the cause of the change in attitude is the fact that when it came to applying this it was very difficult to satisfy everybody. That is human nature. No matter what you do, you will not satisfy everybody. It is an easy thing then, as a solution, to say, "Well, the scheme is no good". I think it is a good scheme as far as it goes. I think the amount is relatively comparable to the need, and if it can be administered in such a way that the benefits will go where they are needed, it will meet the requirements of the fishermen for the time being.
I wish to point out that the prospects for the Newfoundland fishermen are not all dark. Improved methods of fishing are being evolved. We are doing a great deal along this line and we have met with some excellent successes in some cases. Success varies, of course. For example, the federal department in co-operation with the provincial department

-and the two departments work very closely in these things-achieved some very striking results in making the herring fishery in Newfoundland more effective. I should like to quote briefly from a letter I received from a man in the industry, which reads:
We are now conducting a very successful herring season and have caught over 5,000 barrels of green herring in the past three weeks .. . This has given a lot of badly needed employment in this immediate area, as we have 140 men employed with a weekly payroll of over $6,000. These facts, together with the great advantage coming from the roads to resources program over the past few years, are all part of the over-all constructive program of this government.
He branched off from fishing there, but this is a statement contained in a letter with regard to something we were able to do for the herring industry. I might say that in connection with the inshore fishermen-this applies only to inshore fishermen-in 1960 their income was $12,324,881.
What about the physical quantities? That is what the minister gave us in wheat; he did not give us the income.
I do not happen to have the physical quantities. I understood the hon. member to ask for the income and that is what I obtained.
Not I.
In 1961 the figure was $11,045,656, which represents a change downward of $1,279,225.
That is at least 10 per cent.
That is what I said; it is approximately 10 per cent.
I thought the minister said 1 per cent a while ago.

No. I was speaking in connection with the inshore fishermen. Perhaps I neglected to say that, but I was giving the totals for Newfoundland, which were down 1 per cent and included draggers. I have a copy of a telegram from Leslie R. Curtis, acting premier of Newfoundland. This telegram is dated November 21 and reads:
Thank you for your telegram-
The telegram is addressed to the Prime Minister:
-re assistance to fishermen. Newfoundland government will co-operate by contributing 25 per cent of labour cost local public improvement projects as proposed by Premier Smallwood and accepted by you in settlements mutually agreed as requiring assistance. Presume it will be in order now for our nominee to contact your minister of northern affairs and this will be done promptly. Kindest regards.
Leslie R. Curtis
Supply-Fisheries
Mr. Chairman, that is all I wish to say at the present time. I am sorry to have imposed upon the committee for so long and taking up so much of the committee's time.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to add my support to that given by hon. members who have spoken in aid of the fishermen of Newfoundland.
It was very noticeable to those who followed the cod fishery early last summer that the catches were very much below those of the previous year and were below an average catch in many settlements in Newfoundland. On August 24, 1961, Mr. P. J. Antle, general secretary and treasurer of the Newfoundland federation of fishermen, wrote the Minister of Fisheries and on October 4, 1961, the Liberal members from Newfoundland wrote the Minister of Fisheries and indicated their general support for the proposals contained in Mr. Antle's letter.
We were unanimous in our opinion that in dealing with the problem which was facing our fishermen, particularly on the east coast of Newfoundland, the government should be guided by the general principle that our fishermen should be treated in the same way as our mainland farmers when they have a crop failure.
We were well aware that those fishermen who had small catches would find it difficult to provide food for their families, let alone make provision for the next year's cod fishery, which always represents quite an outlay for our fishermen. Very often they have not the means to pay cash for the materials required and have to obtain supplies from their dealers or merchants early in the season in order that they may prosecute the cod fishery.
We suggested in our letter to the Minister of Fisheries that materials be supplied to our fishermen to enable them to build or repair boats and to furnish or repair equipment during the winter months, on the understanding that the fishermen themselves would provide the labour. We thought this would be an extremely practical way to assist those fishermen who are really in need to prepare for their voyages next year. We suggested in our letter:
1.	That this assistance be made available to all fishermen whose total net earnings fell below a certain income, the amount to vary with the number of dependants.
2.	That materials to be supplied include nylon, hemp and cotton twine for knitting of nets and traps; lines and hooks for the making of trawls and bultows; lumber, nails and paint for the building and repairs of

Supply-Fisheries
boats and dories for use in our inshore fishery, and other materials suitable for making moorings for boats and gear.
3.	That the value of such assistance be limited for each fisherman and that the government take a lien on the boats and gear thus provided to ensure that they are used in the fishery for at least one season, after which they would become the property of the fisherman concerned.
The Minister of Fisheries stated that our suggestions had been given full consideration but the committee felt that although assistance in the manner we had proposed would undoubtedly be helpful the problem of dealing with several thousand individual fishermen on an equitable basis would be much less practical than we had suggested. He also said the committee felt that assistance on a community basis directed to those settlements which had been most seriously affected by the catch failure would be more practical and more equitable. With this statement we could not agree. I personally tried to get full details of the assistance which was provided, but I have yet to get it.
On a non-political tour in Newfoundland the Prime Minister announced the response of his government to the appeal of our distressed fishermen. This government was well aware of the catch failure, because the departments concerned were notified by Newfoundland members and, in addition, an official from the Department of Fisheries went to Newfoundland to make an investigation. He obtained the information required and returned to Ottawa.
There seemed to be some confusion as to the number of fishermen affected. If we were to compare the bad fishing of 1961 with the catch in 1960, which was only a fair year, we could conclude that 12,000 fishermen had a bad year in 1961. Anyway, 9,000 fishermen at least and 12,000 fishermen at the most had poor catches. The sum of $300,000 was provided, as announced by the Prime Minister, to aid them. This amount was to be spent on winter works under the same arrangements as those made with regard to all the Canadian provinces from Newfoundland to British Columbia. It meant that if any of our local authorities, municipalities, community councils, local roads boards or any other local organizations carried out public works, half the money spent on labour would be provided by the federal government. In addition, the federal government would match the money provided by the provincial government to the various settlements in respect of road work and so on, since October 15, 1961-a sum which amounted to $80,000. This arrangement meant that the distressed

fishermen from Newfoundland received approximately $20 per family by way of assistance from this government as compared with $1 an acre up to 200 acres or a maximum of $200 in the case of the western farmer.
The minister has referred to just terms. In my opinion Canadians are Canadians irrespective of where they live and they should be treated alike. I am not against assistance being given to our farmers but I contend that the same yardstick which is used for our farmers should be used for our fishermen. The money given to our province was not given to or worked for by fishermen only; it was given to all those who participated in the winter works program. This worked out to about $20 per family-less than three cents a day. While we were glad to get the $300,000 we feel it should have been distributed among our distressed fishermen and that the amount available should have been much greater.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall this item carry?

No, Mr. Chairman. I intend when we resume at nine o'clock to say something about the origins of this policy. I asked the minister to do so but he thought it would take too long. It is going to be done, anyway. I just want to take the minute which is at my disposal now to deal with one point. The minister made a great deal about comparing horses and rabbits. It is obvious that this government regards western farmers as horses and the fishermen as rabbits, though I am surprised the minister should have admitted it.
Headline stuff.
It was not my phrase. It was the phrase of the Minister of Fisheries.
On a point of privilege, I think the hon. member would wish to be fair-
No.
He should admit, I think, that what he has imputed to me was never intended by me. I said that hon. members were not making a fair comparison when they compared things which were not comparable.
Well, there is no dispute between us, and I do not think-
I also said-
I have sat silent all the afternoon. The minister is trying to take the one minute I have on a phony question of privilege. He will find I did not impute anything to him at all.
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member has said-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It is now six o'clock. I therefore regret to interrupt the hon. gentleman but pursuant to the special order made today the proceedings of this committee will be interrupted in order to permit the house to proceed to the consideration of private members' business at eight o'clock.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 8 p.m.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
