subtopic: PROVISION FOR EXTENSION OF FISHING ZONE
PROVISION FOR EXTENSION OF FISHING ZONE
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-3, to amend the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act (12 mile fishing zone).
He said: This particular bill, Mr. Speaker, has two or three general purposes beyond the main one of extending our territorial waters. From what I can gather of at least announced government attitudes, I think these purposes are not inconsistent with the ideas the government has expressed in the past year or so. One of them is to protect our fisheries to the largest possible degree by ensuring (1) that the exploitation and use of our fisheries within the 12 mile area is engaged in by Canadian fishermen and (2) that our conservation practices within that area are not upset by fishermen of other countries coming in and fishing without due regard to the need for conservation as we appreciate it.
A certain aura of government secrecy is involved in this particular question. Since the last Geneva conference on the law of the sea where our efforts were not successful-and just by a small margin, I may say incidentally-no public announcements with any substance to them that I know of have been made by government members with regard to just what has or has not been done by the government itself. In the middle of July last year the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) was asked in the house what action was contemplated by the government with respect to the extension of our territorial waters. The answer he gave at
Coastal Fisheries Protection Act that time hinted-and not too clearly at that -that some talks were perhaps taking place but that the nature of those talks or the wishes and desires of the government were of a confidential nature; hence the house could not be taken into that degree of confidence which is necessary for full understanding of these matters.
Just yesterday a similar question was asked about government activities in this regard and the answer we were given yesterday by the Secretary of State for External Affairs was that it was not beneficial to give an answer. If the government itself would take parliament into its confidence and share some of its ideas with us, perhaps we might not have need to present this particular bill. However, expressing an expectation of the government's taking the house into its confidence in this matter or in most other matters is perhaps asking a little bit too much. None the less, if the government itself would not take this approach of saying in effect, "It is none of your business what we are doing in this field", perhaps we would have slightly better relationships and, as I said, perhaps there would not be any need to introduce a bill of this sort.
However, I suspect that what these announcements made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs in fact mean is that the government is doing nothing about this particular item. It is certainly doing nothing with regard to promotional activities within the United Nations where the initial conference and subsequent conferences were ordered and arranged for. No push or effort or anything of that nature is being promoted within the U.N. toward this particular end. When the Secretary of State for External Affairs says that it is not beneficial to answer questions relating to this matter, I submit he is saying that it is not beneficial to the government because it would be embarrassing for the government to be obliged to admit that it has shelved this most important problem after it did not receive the degree of support we all hoped it would receive at the last conference at Geneva on this matter.
Canada now has a three mile limit. The bill, which is an uncomplicated one to that extent, indicates that for fisheries purposes, we want this limit extended, to 12 miles. The bill also contains another important matter of interest (1) to our fishermen and our fisheries and (2) to our relationships with other countries. Some will say that this bill in fact is asking for a unilateral decision on the part of this parliament and therefore is not concerning itself with the necessity for discussions and negotiations with other countries, because other countries are fishing up to our three mile limit. But this is not the

Coastal Fisheries Protection Act case because there is a very important additional principle contained in the bill to the effect that it will come into force on the first day of July, 1964. The period of two and a half years between now and July 1, 1964, would allow for negotiations to take place with other countries directly, bilaterally, through the United Nations or in some other way, and I intend to mention two or three other methods of entering into some sort of negotiations to solve this problem.
I am a great believer in the approach of negotiation. I do not believe we should take abrupt, unilateral action of a type that will dislocate our relationships with other countries and will tend to dislocate the fishing economies of other countries because I believe we can solve the question much more easily through negotiation. But believing in negotiation I also believe that when you are negotiating you need a good lever on your side in order to ensure that your point of view has the greatest possible impact on the person with whom you are negotiating. The use of a lever in this way often takes place in parliament when the house leaders are negotiating with regard to the business of the house. The matter of whether or not agreement will be reached often depends on whose advantage is served.
The bill contains provisions which permit future action by another parliament depending on the course that negotiations take. If, for argument's sake, international negotiations were under way approaching the first day of July, 1964, when this act would come into force, and it was felt that the negotiations were close to being concluded, a future parliament could easily amend the act to provide for an extension of the date when the bill would come into force so as to permit the negotiations then under way to reach fruition.
The act which the bill seeks to amend, the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act, contains provision in sections 3 and 4 which, even if this amendment is adopted, provide an opportunity for other countries so to adjust their fisheries operations that there will be a minimum amount of dislocation by reason of the coming into force of this amendment. I am sure that the bill before us is based upon government attitudes and ideas as they were last publicly expressed. I have in my hand a green covered booklet. Perhaps its colour is appropriate because it comes from the office of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green). The booklet contains the proposal which Canada made at the first Geneva conference on the law of the sea in 1958 and at the subsequent conference in March, 1960, so far as fishing rights are concerned. I am going


to read from this booklet but the words are also reproduced in the explanatory note in the bill. This was Canada's proposal:
A state has a fishing zone contiguous to its territorial sea extending to a limit 12 nautical miles from the baseline from which the breadth of its territorial sea is measured in which it has the same rights in respect of fishing and the exploitation of the living resources of the sea as it has in its territorial sea.
We took these words at their face value and drafted one of the most important proposed amendments, namely, the definition of what are Canadian territorial waters. We have put these ideas of Canada into legislative form. We regret that the last Geneva conference which dealt with this matter failed by one vote or one third of a vote, as I think the Secretary of State for External Affairs put it, to come to a conclusion with respect to this matter. However, some interesting changes of position were noted at that second conference and I think they afford some area for negotiation by Canada to find a solution for this problem. For instance, we could seek to open negotiations with each or all of the 54 countries who supported our proposal at the second Geneva conference on the law of the sea. At this stage I am not going into the differentiation with regard to the six and six formula that Canada developed. I am confining myself to that part of the formula involving a 12 mile area with regard to fisheries and not the six mile area relating to the territory itself.
We could open negotiations with these 54 countries. We could open negotiations with all the other commonwealth countries who, with the exception of India, supported our proposal at Geneva in 1960. We could negotiate with them to see whether or not an area of agreement might be reached. We could open discussions on the matter with the NATO nations, all of whom except Iceland, and for obvious reasons, I think, agreed with the proposal put forward by Canada in 1960.
With this bill on our statute books I think it would strengthen our hand in any such negotiations. It is most necessary and vital to protect the welfare of our fishing industry and our fishermen. It is most necessary to extend the area of our sovereignty over our own affairs. A former secretary of state for external affairs, the late Sidney Smith, commented on this matter a few years ago and I think it would be appropriate if I were to refer now to what he said. Perhaps at this time we might concern ourselves with putting into effect some of the things which the late Mr. Smith had in mind. As found on page 4353 of Hansard for August 30, 1958, he said:
. .. Canada does not favour the taking of unilateral action by states in respect of fishing zones so long as there is hope that a new international conference

on the law of the sea will he convened in the near future to deal with the question of territorial sea and fishing rights.
With this statement we agree generally. We say that there is no longer hope now, using the words of Mr. Smith, of another international conference on the law of the sea being held in the near future because, first, Canada is not promoting it at the United Nations and, second, so far as I know no other country is promoting it either. In my opinion we should not sacrifice the interests of our fishermen any longer. We should not allow the attitude of the United States in this regard to influence us to the extent that we do nothing about this most important question. This is an all-important matter, and I hope that the house will be kind enough to take one of those rare steps and give second reading to this bill today in order that a humble backbencher may assist the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the government in bringing some relief to citizens of this country.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EXTENSION OF FISHING ZONE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the member for Queens-Lunenburg, where many inshore fishermen as well as many deep sea fishermen derive their living from the sea, I am pleased to speak to this bill to amend the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act. It is interesting to note the attention given this international problem by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard).
The explanatory note of the bill states:
This bill's intent Is that it be a declaration by the Queen in parliament that Canada within those 12 marine miles seaward of her coasts has, to the sole use and benefit of her nationals, the right to fish exclusive of all others: as well an affirmation of Canada's obligation to protect and conserve the live resources of those seas to that same end.
Notwithstanding the remarks of the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard), this bill implies that unilateral action should be taken by the Canadian government in connection with this matter. This course has never been satisfactory when dealing with problems affecting other nations as well as our own. He states that this difficulty would be solved by referring action until July 1, 1964. This, in effect, sets a deadline when all negotiations must cease. I submit to you, sir, this is not a proper course to take.
This problem which the hon. member raises is not a new one. In fact, it goes back to the very beginning of this century. In the 1928 report of the royal commission on fisheries in the maritime provinces we find this at page 90:
The protests of the shore fishermen against steam-trawlers are not new, nor are they wholly the result of conditions prevailing in recent months. They have been persistently and repeatedly made during practically all the years in which steam-
Coastal Fisheries Protection Act trawlers have operated from Nova Scotia ports. A brief outline of the history of these protests may be of interest, as giving a better understanding of the question at issue.
In 1905, when the Halifax board of trade asked for assistance from the federal government to bring out trawlers from Scotland to operate in Nova Scotia, assistance was promptly refused, as indicated by the following letter written on June 5, 1905, by the minister of marine and fisheries at that time, to the chairman of the fisheries committee of the Halifax board of trade:
"Referring the matter of the introduction of steam-trawlers in Atlantic waters of Canada, I have an official report before me, and I do not see that any encouragement could be held out to steam-trawl firms to operate in our waters. You are no doubt aware that to that destructive method of fishing has been attributed the destruction of valuable fisheries off the shores of Great Britain, and prohibitory laws have been enforced in inshore areas. Outside the three mile limit trawling cannot be prevented, but I am not disposed to favour it in territorial waters or grant assistance to firms adopting that method of fishing."
Vigorous protests were made when foreign steam-trawlers began to fish too near to the Atlantic coast line and to interfere with the operations of the shore fishermen; and on September 9, 1908, an order in council was passed providing that "the use or operation of vessels known as steam-trawlers operating beam, otter or other trawls for the purpose of catching fish is prohibited within the three mile limit and in the bays and harbours of Canada." This was obviously an admission that steam-trawling was injuring the shore fisheries, and that it required regulation and restriction. In 1909, during the imperial defence conference, the Canadian minister of marine and fisheries, and the prime minister of Newfoundland urged upon the British government the desirability of making an international arrangement with France and the United States for the regulating of all fisheries on the banks. But no arrangement was made. Protests against steam-trawling, however, continued to be expressed in the maritime provinces, and as a result, the following resolution was passed unanimously by the House of Commons on February 6, 1911:
"That in the opinion of this house, as the mode of fishing known as steam-trawling prosecuted by ships of different nationalities on the coast of Canada outside of Canadian waters is destructive to fish life, it is expedient in order to conserve the deep sea fisheries, that negotiations be opened with the view of securing an international agreement prohibiting this mode of fishing in such spawning grounds for deep sea fish as the waters of the Gulf of St. Lawrence and the banks of the north Atlantic adjacent to the coast of Canada and Newfoundland.
Now, there is considerably more here, Mr. Speaker, but there is one paragraph that I think is most important. I quote again:
On March 18, 1912, the minister of marine and fisheries said in the House of Commons, "If it is possible to do so, effective steps will be taken to prevent steam-trawling being carried on." During the early summer of 1912, a conference was held in Washington, attended by representatives of the United States, by the Canadian minister of marine and fisheries, and by the prime minister of Newfoundland, with a view to investigating the whole question of steam-trawlers and of making observations on the results of their operations. After considerable negotiation, it was arranged that during the season of 1912 investigations would be carried on by each country independently, the understanding being that on the completion of the

Coastal Fisheries Protection Act work, the British government would be asked to call a conference of representatives of countries interested in steam-trawling with a view to reaching an arrangement for the entire prohibition of steam-trawling on this side of the Atlantic. The investigations took longer to complete than was at first anticipated. Meanwhile the war had come. It was then decided to postpone the request for the projected international conference until after the end of the war; but the proposed conference was not held. In order meanwhile to protect further the shore fishermen, the Canadian government in 1915 enacted a regulation under the Customs Act, whereby, the master of any steam-trawler is required before he is granted a clearance for the fishing grounds to give the customs officer a declaration that he will not fish within at least 12 miles from shore, this regulation to apply to all steam-trawlers clearing from a Canadian port on the Atlantic coast, Since that time no further restrictions have been placed on steam-trawlers operating from ports of the maritime provinces.
From this, Mr. Speaker, it can be ascertained that considerable objection was raised against fishing draggers in any area by the inshore as well as the hook and line fishermen on the schooners of that day. This resulted in the prohibition of large Canadian trawlers fishing within 12 miles of shore. Foreign trawlers, of course, are only required to observe the three mile limit. The problem is still of vital interest to our deep sea fishermen as well as to our inshore fishermen. Some time ago, I received a letter from one of our deep sea captains. I should like to place this on the record also for it explains the situation in so far as his operations are concerned;
As master of a Canadian vessel I am very much concerned for myself and my crew over the situation existing at the present time enabling foreign draggers and fishing vessels to fish within the 12 mile limit oH the Nova Scotia coast while we must remain with our draggers outside the 12 mile limit.
The foreign draggers and fishing vessels at certain times of the year are getting the best catches of fish while we are unable to find any satisfactory grounds on which to fish. It is understandable to me that in the interests of international negotiation this situation might be allowed to exist for a very short time but it now already has existed for a long time and in my opinion, and I believe the opinion of most of our fishermen and vessel owners and operators in this area, the time has come when definite action must be taken by our government

At the present time we are unable to find fish outside the 12 mile limit sufficient to make wages for the crew and the foreign draggers are doing well within the 12 mile limit. On our latest fishing trip we sighted at least 35 foreign ships operating within the 12 mile limit, getting large hauls of codfish and flounders, while our Canadian ships had to stay outside and fish for very small hauls of mostly scrod cod. I would like to point out also that the flounders and grey soles and halibut taken by the foreign ships were thrown back as they are not suitable for salting and it appears to us that the present situation is even more ridiculous as we are saving large quantities of fish for the foreigners who are not interested in all the species and destroying the species they do not want.
The area I mention is on the northwest side of Cape St. Lawrence where there is no shore fishery.

The present law might be understandable if there was a shore fishery to protect and I would suggest that if the law is changed any area with a shore fishery should be protected.
Now, conversely-

I said that letter was received some time ago. It is dated May 12, 1959, but the situation is similar today. Conversely, the inshore fisherman with his long-liner has found fish scarce and of necessity, in an effort to secure profitable catches, must go to the off shore banks where he is overly exposed in times of storm. For example, on March 20 last year, some 17 men were lost in one storm when three long-liners failed to return to the port of Lockeport.
However, this problem is somewhat involved. We are concerned here with fishery conservation, which is a matter perturbing many people. We must look at this from many angles. Total fish landings in the maritime provinces during 1961 amounted to 637 million pounds, with a total landed value to our fisherman of $39 million. While fish landings in 1960 were higher, the dollar value was somewhat lower, but during the past three years the average has been approximately $39 million per annum. That is the amount the fishermen have received for their catch.
When we realize that some 18 million Canadians consume on the average only 13 pounds of fish per person per annum we get some idea of the importance of the United States market to our fishing industry. Approximately three quarters of our entire catch is sold in the United States market, and any unilateral action taken by this government to restrict American trawlers from fishing other than 12 miles from shore, would no doubt meet with strong opposition from the United States.
There is another question that poses itself, the question of enforcing unilateral action on a 12 mile limit, and I submit this is of paramount importance. We remember when Iceland in September, 1958, unilaterally declared a 12 mile fishing limit and British trawlers had to be protected by gunboats while they fished off its coast. We also remember that Iceland maintained a fleet of fully armed ships in an effort to enforce its mandatory regulations. Would this be the policy of the C.C.F. and the New Democratic party if they were in office?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EXTENSION OF FISHING ZONE
speechtext: It would be our policy to protect our own fishermen.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EXTENSION OF FISHING ZONE
speechtext:
Certainly it is not the policy of the present administration. However, you may say that Iceland won its dispute with

the United Kingdom, but the Icelandic dispute was not simply between a big power and a little power. It was over a principle that concerns all countries, the principle that the right of states in international law depends upon the consent of other states. Iceland won out over the United Kingdom because the United Kingdom recognized that 99 per cent of the Icelandic economy is tied up in the fishing industry. During that crisis the United Kingdom was placed in a most unenviable position because the western world was concerned lest her action drive Iceland into the communist camp.
At the start of the law of the sea conference in 1958, more countries still upheld the three mile limit than any other single alternative. However, times have changed and at the last law of the sea conference the Canadian proposal that a state has the right to fix the breadth of its territorial sea, up to a limit of six nautical miles, with a fishing zone of an additional six miles, almost met with universal acceptance. I believe the hon. member for Skeena mentioned that it was defeated only by the narrow margin of one vote in failing to get the necessary two thirds majority.
This second law of the sea conference did not reach agreement on the breadth of territorial seas, or on fishing limits, although I still believe the Canadian proposal of six plus six is the best compromise between modern security needs, fishing interests and the fundamental freedom of navigation which all countries have an interest in preserving. Canada is again willing to try at Geneva, or anywhere else. I am quite convinced of that. In our proposals at the last conference on the law of the sea we presented our views in good faith and showed a willingness to co-operate.
Nova Scotians and those associated with the fishing industry generally believe that the search for local compromises is the best way to settle hard cases rather than imposing a flat 12 mile rule.
As I stated earlier, part of the problem is due to a desire to conserve the fisheries and give priority to the coastal fishermen who have a natural wish to increase their catches and raise their standard of living. However, I believe the real answer lies in scientific conservation. With our present knowledge of fish habits and movements we have improved our understanding and ability to tackle the problem, and I think that scientific regulations offer a more effective and skilful system of control than proposals for broad fishing limits that may not, in effect, include the areas most in need of conservation.
This trend of thought receives strong support in international quarters and I believe 26207-1-25
Coastal Fisheries Protection Act at present more countries are in favour of scientific regulation than ever before. There is a sound reason for this type of thinking. In Canada and the United States alone there is a population of over 200 million people, and as the population of the world increases we must constantly turn to the sea for more of our food supplies. We realize that this is the one untapped source available to us. No nation will intentionally destroy this source of protein; all nations will endeavour to preserve the fishing banks in an effort to secure gradually an increasing share of the available catch.
This bill attempts to change the definition of Canadian territorial waters, which limits foreign vessels to a three mile fishing zone. It proposes to change this to a 12 mile zone. Section 4, paragraph (d) of the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act provides that the Governor in Council may make regulations, among other things, designating the territorial waters of Canada for the purpose of the act. In view of this fact it is not necessary to amend it in order to have a 12 mile limit established, as the power is granted to the governor in council to do this at any time.
Present Canadian policy indicates we believe in a clear distinction being made between territorial limits and fishing limits. However, we believe that any change in the fishing limits should be made by universal agreement and must take account of the essential principles of international conduct. The chief of these is the need for international consent prior to any changes being made, because a nation's individual rights are only sustained by general acceptance.
This problem, Mr. Speaker, is still under consideration, but unilateral action as suggested by the bill would only create tensions between Canada and some of its best customers for its fishery products. This would be unacceptable to the Canadian people and I believe undesirable generally to the Canadian fishing industry.

The hon. gentleman deplored the possibility of unilateral action. I do not think anyone wants to have unilateral action. It was the government which preceded the present one which initiated negotiations which were carried on and which almost succeeded, as everyone has pointed out, at Geneva in getting what we wanted by multilateral action. But the fact is that they did not succeed and that so far as we can discover nothing effective has been done since to resume these negotiations.
Yesterday the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) in reply to a question from my hon. friend from Trinity-Conception (Mr. Tucker) who asked whether any negotiations were going on in this matter, said that any such announcement would be made in the house in due course. When the minister was asked by me whether active negotiations were going on at the present time he said:
I think it would not be beneficial to answer that question at this time, Mr. Speaker.
When I was so presumptuous in this free parliament as to ask, "Beneficial to whom?", the minister said, "To Canada. To whom does the hon. member suppose?" The hon. member felt that the minister does not often have a chance to score off anybody any more and the matter could be left there. But the reason for the question was that when this government is not willing to talk about something, I think that is the most conclusive evidence that it is not doing anything, because it spends most of the time talking about things that it is not doing. I think we can fairly assume that the correct answer to, "Beneficial to whom?" was, "To the government", because I cannot believe that, if this government is really seriously carrying on any negotiations, this can be such a deep, dark secret, that those negotiations would be seriously jeopardized if this house were told they were going on.
I would not do what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) did. I would not try to force the government to do what he did-force


Mr. Heath to show the British hand in the common market negotiations, thereby weakening their power to negotiate. I think that just to tell us whether or not the negotiations are going on would do the public interest no conceivable harm and I think we are justified in assuming, until we are told otherwise, that they are not and the government does not want to admit it.
The hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg said this problem was not new. It is not new, that is quite sure. I suppose it is one of the oldest problems. It is as old as Canada and it existed before confederation. It is not a new problem at all but it is a problem that is getting very much worse. I do not need to tell the hon. member for Queens-Lunen-burg, but some hon. members may not be aware of the fact that whereas there were only three or four nations with fishing fleets off the Canadian coast even five or six years ago, ships are coming from all over the world and fishing right off our shores today, and more vested interests-if you like to call them that-more presumptions are being created every year very much to the detriment of the Canadian fishery and Canadian fishermen.
The hon. member also expressed grave concern about the displeasure of the United States. This was very touching coming from a supporter of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and a supporter-I suppose it is still possible to support both the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance, notwithstanding what has been said by a "servile" press. In any event, the proposal was lost and there seems to be no immediate prospect-

That is, by multilateral agreement

If that kind of agreement were not possible, my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition indicated:
The third alternative is for our own government to take unilateral action as other governments have done and decree that there would be a 12 mile fisheries jurisdiction zone laid down in our domestic legislation and that we will exercise jurisdiction in that zone.
That is just what this bill proposes, and that, I may say, is the policy of our party. That is the reason why I have no hesitation in giving support to this bill. I am not very impressed by the dangers which it is suggested might arise from an attempt to enforce this. After all, if Iceland and Norway have been able to do this by unilateral action it is hard to persuade me that the Canadian people, if they had a resolute government which could make up its mind about anything, would have any difficulty in doing the same.
There is plenty of time left to have a vote on this bill and I hope we can have a vote before nine o'clock.

He is going to the Liberal dinner.
He seems to be a man who has done everything in the past. He and his friends look at every effort ever made by this government, every law that has ever been enacted, and they say: we did that in the past; we prepared legislation of that kind, or, in this case: we prepared submissions to Geneva. I can imagine attending the conference on the law of the sea at Geneva. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate walks into the hall brandishing a Canadian ultimatum,

and I can see all the representatives of all other countries bowing and saying: yes, we accede to the request of the representative from Canada. I find it hard to understand how either the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) or the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate can tell us that they do not foresee clearly that the result of this bill must be unilateral action. They wish to change paragraph (b) of section 2 of the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act so as to read:
'Canadian territorial waters' means a fishing zone extending seaward to a limit 12 nautical miles from the baseline from which the breadth of the territorial seas of Canada are measured, and includes inland waters of Canada.
In the explanatory notes it is stated that to allow time for international negotiation which might result in agreement on national fishing limits, the bill is deferred in effect until July 1, 1964. Despite this provision, however, I believe that this measure definitely represents unilateral action and in all circumstances I do not believe anyone would wish that Canada should go to that extent. I agree that it is necessary to protect our fishing zones by the conservation and preservation of the species of fish. There is a special threat on the east coast where we see many ships from foreign countries, including factory ships, taking fish three miles from the Canadian coast. However, is it not best that we should settle this question by negotiation-negotiation, for example, with our neighbour to the south-although the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate seems to be a great enemy of our neighbour to the south?
