subtopic: PROVISION FOR EXTENSION OF FISHING ZONE
speechtext: Some formula has to be found. Norway and Britain found a formula at their meeting in Oslo in 1960; since that period a four mile fishing limit was progressively extended into a 12 mile fishing zone. This is one example of negotiations between two countries successfully reaching a conclusion on this matter. I think the Canadian people would not wish to say that there must be both a 12 mile fishing limit and a 12 mile territorial zone. It might be better to suggest that we should have a three mile territorial zone and a 12 mile fishing zone. If we were to say this, it is possible that negotiations with many of the other countries would be successful and we would attain our objective, not by means of an ultimatum such as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate suggests but through friendly relations. I regret that I cannot endorse this bill as it is presented to us, though if it were amended we could possibly come to some understanding and to better terms.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EXTENSION OF FISHING ZONE
speechtext:
The hour for the consideration for private members' business having expired, the house will resume the business which was interrupted at eight o'clock.

The house again in committee of supply, Mr. Martineau in the chair.

Special-
612. Contribution towards a special Newfoundland works program for fishing settlements that experienced income reduction resulting from decreased catches, $300,000.

When the committee rose at six o'clock I had just begun to say something about the observation that had been made by the Minister of Fisheries and, particularly his appeal that we should make fair comparisons. I suggested that the kind of comparisons the minister himself was making were not fair comparisons. What I really rose to say first of all was that the minister threw up his hands at the possibility of doing anything for the fishermen comparable to what was done under the acreage payment scheme which we had previously voted for the wheat growers and grain growers of the west. The minister suggested that the problem of the fishermen was far too complicated for a similar solution, and that the difficulties were far too great. I cannot imagine that the minister really meant that. It would be much easier indeed to apply to the fishermen of Newfoundland-and I refer to the inshore fishermen of Newfoundland-a system such as that which we just adopted for the farmers of western Canada than to apply it to the farmers of western Canada. We already have in existence all the required administrative machinery to make that procedure possible and I am going to tell the minister just exactly how it could be done, just as I told the Prime Minister in 1958 how it could be done.
The machinery is there. It is there in the unemployment insurance commission. All the fishermen who would be concerned are insured under the unemployment insurance commission. Their files are there. The number of stamps they have is known to the commission. From its own records already available to it the government would have no difficulty whatsoever in identifying them and segregating those who were bona fide fishermen. They could have made such payments in two simple ways. They could have said, "We are going to give $200 for income maintenance to the western farmers who have had a crop failure, though in fact, crop failure, as the Acting Minister of Agriculture has told us, was taken care of under the Prairie Farm
Supply-Fisheries
Assistance Act which has no parallel whatever with the fishermen. This income maintenance was provided to the prairie farmers on two occasions when there was not a crop failure. I refer to the year 1958 and the year 1960. One way to have paid the fishermen was to do what was done with the prairie farmers, namely to say that, regardless of what their crop was, everyone of them would get the payment and the payment could have been a flat $200. I am not saying that I would have advocated that method. The minister said it could not be done. I say that it could have been done very easily. There would not have been the slightest difficulty in doing it. It could have been done in a very few weeks without encountering any problem whatsoever in an administrative sense. The minister has fisheries officers who know very well who the fishermen are.
It could be done in another way. It could be done on a graduated basis depending on how many stamps the fishermen had, so that those who had a good catch and had a sufficient number of stamps and therefore did not need any special help would not get it and it would go only to those who, because of their poor catch, were qualified to get it. That would be to apply a limited kind of test of need, something which was not done in the case of the western farmers. However, that is something that could have been done. These are two ways in which payments could have been made and by means of which the fishermen could have been treated in exactly the same way as the farmers were treated.
Why was this not done? I do not know. It would not have cost much money, whichever method had been followed. If anybody thinks that income maintenance is not just as necessary for the fishermen as it is for the farmers, I should just like him to compare their income levels and say that to any fisherman on the east coast.
May I ask the hon. gentleman a question?
Certainly.

I, too, believe in the sincerity of the fishermen but if he proposes to this committee that any fisherman- who has not earned sufficient stamps should qualify for unemployment insurance benefits during the winter months, how can be prove that this fisherman tried to fish? Could he not just sit at home?

I can answer that question. You could eliminate any fisherman who did not have a reasonable number of stamps the previous year. That would be a fairly good test, if you are so anxious to screw the fishermen down. Nobody heard the hon. member

Supply-Fisheries
get to his feet and suggest tests like that for the western farmers. Why is there this desperate concern about a few dollars going to the fishermen after we have voted $42 million to the western farmers? That is exactly the question we are asking. We willingly voted this money to the western farmers because we thought they needed it. However, we think the fishermen need it also. It is rather hard to go down and tell the fishermen that the only way in which they can get it is to get jobs and sweat it out on work on the roads in the winter time at $20 when the western farmer gets a cheque for $200 from Alvin's cheque machine. That is what this government is asking the fishermen to accept. That is a perfectly fair and valid comparison. Whether or not it is fair or valid, it is a comparison which the fishermen in every settlement in Newfoundland make. If anyone doubts it, let him go down and ask them. I know the situation. I have heard them make the comparison.
You want a police state.

I want a little bit of fairness and a little bit of equality. The hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine who interrupted me a little while ago, at the conclusion of his speech, said that if we could suggest some simple method by which the fishermen could be aided as the farmers were aided, he would support it. I have suggested two simple methods by which it could be done. I hope he will rise in his place and support them.
It is not sensible.

Go and tell that to the fishermen. I certainly would not tell the fishermen that it is fair that the western farmers should receive P.F.A.A. cheques if they have complete crop failures and in addition to that get another $200, while the fisherman, if he can get one of these jobs on one of these works projects, gets $20. I would not want to go around and tell them that. If the members of this government want to do so they are perfectly welcome to do it.
Do you know that the farmers paid in to P.F.A.A.?
How much?

All I am suggesting is this. I admit right away what the minister said. I admit that you cannot have absolute mathematical equality. We did not have it in the acreage payments and the government did not make any such pretension. In no scheme which you have in effect to deal with this problem can you have it either. But in this way you could do something roughly comparable and it would be administratively quite easy to do.

The minister suggested that this scheme which we now have before us, as envisaged in this $300,000 vote, was what was suggested by the Newfoundland federation of fishermen last August. I think we really ought to look at what the Newfoundland federation of fishermen themselves said and not at the interpretation placed upon it by the minister. I should like to read from a letter sent by them to the minister of which I have a copy.
What is the date of the letter?

The date of the letter is August 24, 1961. There are two or three points about the date that I wish to draw particularly to the attention of hon. gentlemen opposite. The general secretary treasurer of the Newfoundland federation of fishermen, Mr. P. J. Antle, wrote as follows:
It Is now apparent that the Inshore fishery In Newfoundland has been a complete failure, due entirely to the scarcity of codfish. This disaster as it can be rightly described applies to fishermen all around the province. In a few areas a small number of fishermen did secure fair catches and obtained sufficient stamps to qualify for unemployment insurance benefits.
Just as a few farmers had bumper crops, but there were not many of them; and there certainly were not many fishermen who in August, at any rate, were in this category, although some of them may have improved their situation later in the year. The letter continues:
The same general scarcity of fish still prevails and hopes for a successful fall fishery are fading day by day.
This was in August. That is when the government was warned about this problem and I want to emphasize that point. The letter continues:
Thousands of our fishermen do a little subsistence farming and produce sufficient vegetables for local consumption. In normal years production of vegetables helped to supplement earnings from the fisheries. As a result of the long dry summer those precious crops were stunted or ruined completely. In addition many fishermen due to forest fires are precluded from augmenting their income from fall employment in the woods industry.
The combination of disasters has left the great majority of our fishermen in desperate economic conditions. These conditions will grow worse with the approach of winter.
The letter continues:
On behalf of our fishermen I am appealing to you, and through you to the federal government for some form of special assistance to help them through the winter.
"Some form".
I will not attempt to outline the nature or form of such special assistance.
I am not accusing the minister of bad faith; I am just saying that the minister

did not correctly interpret this letter. Contrary to what the minister said, Mr. Antle did not say there must be works. He said:
I will not attempt to outline the nature or form of such special assistance. Men in your department more capable and with far more experience than I are best qualified to deal with such matters. However, I would suggest a continuation of community stage development, building or repairing of access roads to fishing communities and an expanded program of public works such as the construction of wharves and breakwaters.
This was just one suggestion, but it was the assistance for which they were appealing.
A further subject for study would be some form of loan program for Inshore fishermen to enable them to engage in next year's fishery with adequate fishing equipment.
It was because of that phrase in that letter and the knowledge and experience that my friends from Newfoundland on this side of the house had of this situation that we ventured jointly to write a letter to the minister which was described by two of my colleagues in the course of their speeches and in which we made a very practical suggestion which the minister said looked fine until it was examined. But I cannot believe that the minister's department is so devoid of administrative capacity that if they had really wanted to accept this suggestion it would not have been quite possible to do so. They have fishery officers who during the winter months could very well have supervised this program and could very well have made sure that the materials provided were used for the purpose for which they were provided. The scheme was thoroughly practical, thoroughly simple and bound to help the fishermen. Then Mr. Antle went on to say:
Such program would necessitate a combined effort on the part of the Department of Fisheries, the Department of Public Works and the provincial government of Newfoundland.
That was August 24. There was not a word from the government all through the concluding part of last session. I must say that I fully expected that with that appeal from Mr. Antle and with the knowledge which the ministers in the government had, which I am sure was communicated to them by their distinguished colleague from Newfoundland, some special assistance would be provided in the concluding part of the last session of parliament which was held in September. But not a word did we hear.
Could I ask the hon. gentleman a question?
Certainly.

Did he have any request from the premier of Newfoundland or the minister of fisheries of Newfoundland?
Supply-Fisheries

No, sir, I did not have any request from them. I have read the constitution of Canada a good many times and I know that it is not in section 92 but in section 91 that jurisdiction exists over fisheries, and so does the minister. This is a national problem, something that is under the jurisdiction of parliament, not under the jurisdiction of the provincial government, and it should have been tackled by parliament in the same way that the wheat acreage payments were. There were no requests from provincial governments for acreage payments at all. That was done by the federal government on its own motion and the same treatment should have been accorded to the fishermen.
Agriculture is a joint responsibility of the federal and provincial governments. The fisheries are an exclusive responsibility of the federal government. Yet the minister from Newfoundland gets up and says, "Did you have any request from the premier"? It is not the premier's business; it is the business of the Solicitor General. That is what he is in the cabinet for, to put forward the claims of the people of Newfoundland. I should like to ask him what he did about it when this letter came. I hope that when I have concluded he will tell us about his gallant efforts on behalf of the fishermen, getting $20 a head for the fishermen when his colleague from Saskatchewan was getting $200 a head for the farmers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: How much did you get?
If that is the way he is going to fight the next election, I do not mind when it comes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: How much did you get?

I could tell the hon. gentleman that but it is not relevant to this debate. I am not going to be put off by any diversion from the hon. gentleman whose knowledge of fishing is, I imagine, greater than mine, but has nothing to do with the kind of fishing about which we are now talking.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You are pretty easily put off.

There was not a word about this from the federal government from August 24 until October 19. What was the brilliant way they intended to deal with it then? Did they bring forward a program of their own? I should like to read a message, of which I have a copy, which represents the first action by this government, two months after they were told that this problem was urgent and that it should be dealt with in the fall and not in the winter. On October 19 we have this message to the premier of Newfoundland from the Prime Minister of Canada:

Supply-Fisheries
The dominion government has been considering the difficulties of those fishing communities in Newfoundland which have suffered severely from the poor catch this year and we feel there are opportunities for providing needed assistance by taking advantage promptly of opportunities and funds now available under the municipal winter works program which is applicable to the local road boards in unorganized Newfoundland communities. I would suggest your government consider immediately working out with us arrangements to apply this program in outport communities where employment is needed. Please let me hear from you as soon as possible.
I have the reply of the premier of Newfoundland to that message and as I think it expresses the position more simply than I could paraphrase it I will read it. It is dated October 26, 1961 and is addressed to the Prime Minister:
My dear Prime Minister:
Thank you for your telegram of October 19 in which you say your government has been considering the difficulties of those fishing communities in Newfoundland which have suffered severely from the poor catch this year. You suggest taking advantage of opportunities and funds available under the municipal winter works program through local road boards where there are no municipal councils. We have carefully considered this suggestion but there are two almost insuperable difficulties. First, we could not in such winter works possibly discriminate between fishermen and other persons who might be equally in need and second, as your fisheries officers will confirm, the fishermen in question are scattered through some 600 settlements along 4,000 miles of coast and the administrative difficulties of organizing projects on such a scale with the limited facilities available for supervision hardly need any emphasis.
We suggest-
This was a counter suggestion made by the premier.
-as a more feasible alternative that the federal government consider organizing through its fisheries officers and the public works department-
Not through the provincial government and the local road boards. In other words, Mr. Smallwood was simply saying that the federal government should mind its own business and do its own business.
We suggest as a more feasible alternative that the federal government consider organizing through its fisheries officers and public works department, a series of small marine projects such as fishermen's slipways, wharves and small breakwaters of which your public works department already has rough plans available-
I know they have lots of them.
-and that such projects be started and carried on as far as conveniently possible during the winter and early spring. Such a federal program, because of the constitutional responsibility of the federal government of Canada, could be done exclusively for fishermen and supervised jointly by your public works department and fisheries officers As such projects would undoubtedly provide some financial relief to our welfare department we would be prepared to provide 25 per cent of the labour costs-

You will see the reason why this provision is made. The premier felt that if nothing was done the welfare costs incurred by the province would be greater and that if some of these projects were undertaken there would be a saving in one respect to the province and they would have this money which they could use to pay part of the labour costs.
The letter continues:
As such projects would undoubtedly provide some financial relief to our welfare department we would be prepared to provide 25 per cent of the labour costs of any such projects undertaken during the winter and spring, notwithstanding the fact that such undertakings would be exclusively in the field of activity as signed by the constitution to the government of Canada.
Now, here was something that was entirely the business of the government of Canada and no business of the provincial government at all. The Prime Minister tried to pass the buck to the province. The premier pointed out, and pointed out very considerately, courteously and respectfully, that it would not work and why it could not possibly work. In order to be constructive he put forward an alternative, something that any self-respecting national government would have done on its own. In order to be as conciliatory as possible the provincial government offered to pay part of the labour costs.
What happened after that? The Prime Minister sent another message, and I think the real story of this vote should be on the record. I am sorry the minister did not see fit to place it on the record. We should know what really did happen. The Prime Minister, on November 3, sent a further message to the premier in which he said:
Reurlet October 26 assistance to fishermen would like to clarify October 19 proposal. I do not believe that there will be any possible discrimination since any settlement incorporated or unincorporated anywhere in the province is eligible under winter works incentive program to secure grant equal to amount provided by your government for labour in annual road building grants. Understand such grants made to five hundred seventy five settlements last year under administration of your department of highways. If plan accepted all settlements can double their work programs at no additional cost to your government. Urgently request you to authorize representative to act during your absence to work out details of this practical program with this government.
I do not know who on earth advised the Prime Minister of Canada to send that message to the premier of Newfoundland. Whoever it was knew nothing about Newfoundland, nothing whatever. In the first place, what are these local road programs? They are programs that are carried on normally in the summer and fall. They are not winter works at all. Most of that money had already been spent long before that telegram was sent. Moreover, these works are works for

the whole community and no government would dare to say that only fishermen could be employed on them or that other people who were not fishermen could not be employed, as the premier had already pointed out. As a matter of fact, whoever the Prime Minister may have consulted about this, I may say it was about as foolish a message as could possibly have been sent.
In the meantime, the premier of Newfoundland had gone overseas on provincial business and the acting premier replied to this telegram. In order to make the story complete, sir, I should like to read the reply. It is dated November 8, and reads as follows:
Retel am wondering whether it is clearly understood by government of Canada that local road grants for present year referred to were made during the spring and summer and that practically all allocations totalling approximately four hundred thousand dollars regular grant and one hundred thousand supplementary grants for special needs have now been expended. Are we to understand from your telegram that government of Canada is prepared to match this amount which has already been expended by our local road boards without further cost to the government of Newfoundland.
Now, that is very important. In the settlements where the money had already been spent, was the federal government going to spend the same amount without cost to the provincial government? That is what the acting premier is asking.
Would appreciate your confirmation that this is so.
Then, he sent a letter in some detail which I will not weary the committee by reading, incorporating the telegram and, for greater certainty, expanding on this program. I have here a copy of a document prepared by the acting premier who, when he furnished me with a copy of this letter, wrote:
After the foregoing message was sent to the Prime Minister Honourable W. J. Browne made a statement. The report I heard over the air stated that according to Mr. Browne the federal government had turned down a suggestion by Premier Smallwood. They would, however, be considering at an early date a proposition put forward by the attorney general.
In order to make it quite clear that my telegram was not to be considered as other than an inquiry I addressed the attached letter to the Prime Minister.
That is the letter to which I refer.
Perhaps you had better read it.

The minister suggests that I should read it. I am quite prepared to read it if the minister really wants me to do so. I am sure the minister is very familiar with the contents. They bear out completely what was said. It is dated November 10, and the first part of it reads:
Supply-Fisheries
This will confirm my telegram to you dated the 8th inst. with reference to your correspondence with Premier Smallwood re assistance to fishermen.
Then, the telegram is again given verbatim and I will not read it a second time. The letter continues as follows:
Before Premier Smallwood left for Europe he asked me to handle this matter in his absence: but before authorizing an expenditure of between one quarter and one half a million dollars, I wanted to be quite sure that there would be no misunderstanding between the government of Canada on the one hand and the government of Newfoundland on the other.
Your telegram of the 3rd instant states that any settlement, incorporated or unincorporated anywhere in the province is eligible under winter works incentive program to secure a grant equal to the amount provided by your government for labour in annual road building grants. The amount appropriated by the Newfoundland government to five hundred and twenty-four settlements this year was approximately $400,000. being $2 per capita of the population of each area. In addition, an amount of $100,000 was appropriated for special works, such as local bridges, etc. We have been trying to find out how much of this money was spent in materials and for hire and how much in labour. It would seem from the tabulations already prepared (and many returns are not yet in) that the amount for labour would be about 75 per cent of the various allocations. Of course the amount would vary from settlement to settlement according to the nature of the work done.
If I interpret your telegram of November 3, correctly it would seem to me that your government is now offering these various road boards approximately 75 per cent of the amount of their annual grant, or roughly $300,000, and I have given instructions to the department of highways to be ready to notify the road boards concerned that this additional money is available as soon as my interpretation is confirmed.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I am sorry, but I have to advise the hon. gentleman that his time has expired.
Perhaps for the sake of continuity, the committee might consider permitting me to finish reading the letter.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Does the committee give unanimous consent to the hon. member continuing his quotation?
Agreed.

I continue the quotation:
The regular practice in allocating road board moneys is for the road boards concerned to call a public meeting of the settlement and to put before that meeting a program of expenditure which must be approved by that meeting before any funds are allocated by the government. In that way the public has some control over expenditure. In view of the lateness of the season it would seem that the various road boards will have to be left on their own to decide how and where these additional moneys, if available, are to be spent.
I am sure the various settlements will appreciate the expenditure in their areas of these additional moneys, but I doubt very much if the expenditure of $1.50 per capita in any community (and that figure would seem to represent the labour share of our annual road grants), would be of any substantial assistance to fishermen in a small community.

Supply-Fisheries
Then, there is the usual appropriate conclusion. Since my time has expired, sir, I will reserve my other remarks until some other hon. gentleman has spoken.

I had not intended to take part in this debate but the remarks made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate have cast what I consider to be an unfair reflection on some of the people I represent and on some of the policies brought forward by this government, and the former government of which he was a member, to provide assistance for the people in my area.
I am sure the fishermen of Newfoundland would not wish to be associated with any misrepresentation made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. The Prairie Farm Assistance Act is a measure which was introduced to relieve distress caused by drought and crop failure in the wheat growing regions of western Canada.
By a Liberal government.

I am proud to acknowledge that fact and to say this government improved on that legislation. It provides that on each bushel of grain delivered to the grain elevators by farmers in western Canada, there is a levy imposed, deducted, and put in a fund and that fund, assisted by the treasury of Canada, is used to pay awards to those farmers who qualify after their crops have been inspected and it has been determined that they have suffered through crop failure.
The acreage payment is, of course, another matter, being in the nature of a subsidy to Canadian consumers of bread. From its introduction in 1958 it was considered in that respect, and it has absolutely no similarity to a drought payment, so far as the farmers of western Canada are concerned. I hope the fishermen in Newfoundland will pardon me for interrupting a debate in which I know they are vitally interested, but I thought that on behalf of my own constituents I should make this correction of the facts that have been placed before us today.

I am most grateful to the hon. member for Rosthern and I have no quarrel with one word he has said. I am just as proud of the P.F.A.A. as he is. I am proud of the fact it was introduced by a Liberal government and I only wish something similar existed for the benefit of the fishermen.
May I ask the hon. member a question?
I really have a lot of things I want to say about the fishermen, and I deliberately refrained from bringing the fishermen into the debate on the acreage payments.
I should like to ask a question.

Perhaps the hon. member could ask it when I have concluded. I would prefer to continue my remarks and conclude the account of what actually did happen about this matter. There were one or two more communications and I do not want anyone to say that I have left out any part of the record.
On November 15 the Prime Minister replied to these communications, the letter and the telegram, and he said:
Dear Mr. Curtis:
While I will be absent for a couple of days I wish at once to acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 10th instant which just came into my office this afternoon.
I will turn your letter over to the Minister of Northern Affairs for his immediate attention.
I am not quite sure why it was the "Minister of Northern Affairs", but that is what the letter says. Then, on November 21, the Prime Minister sent a telegram to Mr. Curtis, the acting premier, which reads as follows:
With further reference problem certain fishing settlements where fisherman had poor results in fishing season we are prepared through winter works incentive program to match labour content of all local road boards grants eligible under that program and possibly including work done since October 15th.
I direct the attention of members to that. It is very different from the first brave offer, which said they were going to match all of the road grants for the whole season, but when the facts began to trickle slowly down in Ottawa they reneged on that offer and said "Oh, no, we will only match those in the settlements where the money has not been spent, possibly including work done since October 15." In that way a settlement in which the people had energetically got their road work done would not get any benefit. That is part of the history of nondiscriminatory, practical policy suggested by hon. gentlemen opposite to deal with the problem. The telegram continues:
Where such expenditure fails to meet need we are prepared to provide additional funds up to $300,000 for local public improvement projects capable of being carried out by March 31st, 1962, in fishing settlements mutually agreed as requiring assistance provided your government will contribute 25 per cent of labour cost as suggested premier's letter October 26th.
In other words, the federal government was not willing to assume its own responsibilities and do the job itself. It insisted on getting the last nickel it could get out of the treasury of Newfoundland, to deal with a national problem that was its responsibility.
I have another message from Mr. Curtis to the Prime Minister. It is the same date, November 21, and is as follows:

Thank you for your telegram re assistance to fishermen. Newfoundland government will co-operate by contributing 25 per cent of labour cost local public improvement projects as proposed by Premier Smallwood-
This was the same scheme as the Solicitor General said they had already turned down.
-and accepted by you in settlements mutually agreed as requiring assistance. Presume it will be in order now for our nominee to contact your Minister of Northern Affairs and this will be done promptly. Kindest regards.
Then there is one other message, from the Prime Minister to Mr. Curtis, dated November 24, 1961. This spanned the period from August to September, one month; September to October two months, and October to November; three months after Mr. Antle brought this urgent matter to the attention of the government. It was three months before anything got off the ground because of the buck passing performance that had been carried on. The message reads as follows:
Thank you for your message of the 21st accepting our proposal re assistance to fishermen. Will advise you Friday names of our officials designated to confer with your nominee.
I would draw attention to the fact that all Mr. Curtis accepted, all he had agreed to was to co-operate by contributing 25 per cent of the labour cost. This was a federal scheme. This $300,000 was federal money and towards that scheme the provincial government said it would contribute 25 per cent of the labour cost.
I have not got any further documentary evidence and I prefer to speak only about those things that I really know, but I have read what took place in the legislature. Indeed, I was present in the house on December 4 when this was first discussed, but the latest statement that has come to my attention is a quite recent one which I should like to put on the record. It is from the St. John's daily News of January 16, 1962. In it there is an article headed:
Federal winter works aid misunderstood-blame lies with Ottawa.
Throughout Newfoundland there seems to be quite a bit of misunderstanding about the federal government's winter works for the distressed fishermen.
In an announcement yesterday, the Premier said that some people do not seem to understand that this whole scheme belongs to the federal government at Ottawa.
"The Newfoundland government do not like it." the premier declared, "and have said so very plainly.
Indeed, some of the things he said in the legislature were not very flattering. However, the article continues:
"I denounced it strongly in the House of Assembly, and so did everyone else in the Newfoundland government."
Supply-Fisheries
Another part of the article reports the premier as follows:
"The Canadian government officials came to St. John's from Ottawa and planned out the whole scheme," Mr. Smallwood continued.
"They decided what place along the seacoast should receive anything from the winter works program. They picked out the very settlements where this scheme would be carried out. They decided how much money would be sent to each individual settlement.
The Newfoundland government had nothing whatsoever to do with selecting the bays or settlements, or anything to do with deciding how much money would be sent to each place".
Concerning the money from Ottawa, the premier had this to say: "The Newfoundland government were asked if they would permit the money provided by Ottawa to be sent to the local boards in the various settlements-the town councils, community councils, local road boards, etc. The Newfoundland government agreed that the money could be sent to those organizations but the Newfoundland government refused point blank to decide how the money should be spent".
That is all that is in direct quotation marks and therefore that is all with which I think I should weary the committee. I wish to make a few very brief observations. As my hon. friend from Burin-Burgeo said when he opened the discussion of this estimate, notwithstanding the inequity, notwithstanding the impossibility of deciding whether this aid would go to fishermen or to other persons in the settlements, notwithstanding the difficulties of administration and the inadequacy of the road boards, with the best will in the world, to administer this kind of program, particularly when it was delayed for three unnecessary months from August until November, if this government was prepared to do nothing else, in view of the very serious crop failure of the fishermen this is better than nothing and we are not going to be so foolish as to refuse it.
But when we apply to it the test-and I quote the words of the Minister of Fisheries as I took them down-which we ought to apply, being completely fair, with complete fairness and justice to all-those were the words which I copied down as the minister uttered them-and consider that the whole thing is rubbed in by asking us to vote this money immediately after the acreage payments, the discrepancy is so frightful that it is hard to believe that the government had any notion at all of the kind of problem with which they were dealing.
There was no reason on earth why the federal government should not in August, when that letter came, have sent Mr. McArthur or one of the other capable people they have in the department to Newfoundland and on their own responsibility produced a thoroughly workable scheme for dealing with this problem. It is a national problem which under our constitution belongs to this

Supply-Fisheries
parliament and not to the legislature. The government should have done this instead of offering winter works. These same winter works were offered the winter before and the winter before that. They were available on exactly the same terms. The original offer of October 19 was absolutely nothing that was not already there for any other province which did not have this crop failure.
It was only when the premier of Newfoundland stirred them up by saying that Newfoundland, though it needs every dollar in its treasury for provincial purposes, would help this great federal government in a scheme if they would get a scheme started and do it themselves, that we got anything at all; and still we got something that is a hit or miss, haphazard arrangement. You cannot tell whether the aid really goes to the fishermen or not.
Perhaps it should not. It is hard to go into one of these communities where a man who is not a fisherman needs a job just as badly as one who is a fisherman, and say to the one who is a fisherman, "You can have a job" and to the one who is not a fisherman, "You cannot". I should not like to do that and I should not like to be part of the government which foisted that kind of policy upon the local authorities and road boards. That was not done to the farmers, as my hon. friend from Burin-Burgeo pointed out. The farmers did not have to go out and work for their $200. They received a cheque. Why should not the fishermen be treated in the same way as the farmers?
Mr. Antle said they did not want a handout.
Oh, the Solicitor General calls what the government has given to the farmers a handout.
I said that was what Mr. Antle said.
The minister said the fishermen did not want a handout. In other words, he is calling the acreage payments a handout.
On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, I said to the hon. member that Mr. Antle, whom the hon. member quoted, said they did not want handouts. He wrote that himself.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Acreage payments are not handouts at all.

If acreage payments are not handouts, why would a payment to the fishermen be a handout, because the problem of a deficiency of income was precisely the same in both cases. It was a crop failure

in both cases. Why is it not a handout if it is paid to the farmer, and is a handout if it is paid to the fisherman? I cannot understand it, and neither can any reasonable man in Newfoundland or anywhere else.
In any event, Mr. Antle said-unfortunately I sent his letter to Hansard so I cannot quote his sentence verbatim-that it was up to the federal government to decide what was the best method of assistance. He did make a few suggestions, but he was not trying to govern Canada. Do not try to pass the buck to Mr. Antle, as you tried unsuccessfully to pass it to the premier of Newfoundland. It was the responsibility of these hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches who were given a huge majority to govern Canada, and who refuse to deal with any problem that arises, in any constructive fashion. I have been given a copy of Mr. Antle's letter and I think it is worth reading again what he said.
Mr. Chairman, I did not say it was in his letter. I said that he made that statement in the Newfoundland Fisherman, the magazine published by the Newfoundland federation of fishermen.

I am sure the Solicitor General knows just as well as I what Mr. Antle meant. He meant that the fishermen did not want to have to go on relief. The Solicitor General's leader promised that no one in Canada would have to go on relief if they voted for him in 1958. I have the promise right here.
That is not true.

That is what was meant by a handout. They meant they wanted to be treated like any other Canadian and not driven on to relief. But hon. gentlemen opposite prefer to give them $20 and let them go on relief. That is their policy, and it does not wash. It is not good enough. If that is their conception of complete fairness and justice to all-
It is a lot better than you did.
The hon. gentleman says, "It is a lot better than you did". I also read-

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: So right.

A short time ago I read the Prime Minister's promise at Yarmouth, that there would be price supports for the fishermen as there are for the farmers, with the price known at the beginning of the season. Has that happened in the last four years since the promise was made? It is all of a piece, sir.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: You have only Newfoundland members in the committee now.
I know the hon. gentleman is not very much interested in Newfoundland-that is very evident-and neither are the rest of his colleagues.

You are
monopolizing all the time.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Five members from Newfoundland; nobody else.

On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, the Solicitor General said I was monopolizing all the time. This debate started before four o'clock this afternoon and I did not rise until two minutes to six o'clock, so that anyone who says I have monopolized all the time is absolutely incorrect. Before I intervened in the debate I waited until every other hon. member who wanted to speak had an opportunity to do so. I represent a very large number of fishermen who had a crop failure last year. I was elected to represent these people and I intend to represent them and support them, and not make excuses for the failure of this government to accept its responsibilities and discharge them seriously and fairly.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Are you going to have a convention this time too?

The hon. gentleman is worried about a convention. If he would like to come down and represent his party, which has never had a convention in my constituency, I think his fate would not be different from that of his predecessors. I would not, if I were the hon. gentleman, talk very much about that subject. In any event, like most of the other interventions from the other side of the house, it is altogether irrelevant to the vote before us. If this is all the government will do-if they are not shamed into doing something better-it is still a pittance; it still is something, and nobody is going to refuse it.

There are a few remarks I should like to make. I do not intend to detain the committee long, because it may feel inclined to pass this item before it rises. I should like to point out, as I have said before, that as far as the income of inshore fishermen in Newfoundland is concerned, in 1961 it was 1 per cent less than the three year average and for 1961 as compared with 1960 it showed a decline of a little more than $1 million-about $1,250,000 in round figures, or approximately 10 per cent as compared with 1960-and 1960 was one of the best income years that the fishermen of Newfoundland had experienced since union,
Supply-Fisheries
since the time when the federal Department of Fisheries undertook its responsibility toward Newfoundland.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate has poured scorn on the negotiations which began very shortly after the first request for assistance was made, and which were carried out by officials of my department. I do not want to name individuals, but some of the groups included Mr. McArthur to whom the hon. member referred. They went down to Newfoundland and conferred with representatives of the industry and of the provincial government. Afterwards they came up with the advice on which this program was based. The hon. member for Bon-avista-Twillingate has said that anyone who could persuade the Prime Minister to write such a letter was foolish-that it was utter nonsense and he was displaying his ignorance of the situation in Newfoundland. I have advisers in my department who, I believe, are second to none among civil servants who are fisheries experts anywhere in the world. I say that they take second place to no one in the federal service, and on their advice and with the best judgment I could muster I made those recommendations and I take full responsibility for them. I do not say for one moment, nor do I pretend to say that my intimate knowledge of the fisheries of Newfoundland is great, but at least I am a neighbour of Newfoundland and I am an east coaster familiar with the environment in which the fishermen live. Small as my knowledge may be I do not intend that it should be overridden by the vast lack of knowledge displayed by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
I have proposed this item to this committee on the basis of the best advice available, with the cheerful co-operation of the officials and of the government of Newfoundland up to a certain point-about the day the legislature opened. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate has admitted he was there on that day. Then the attitude of the provincial government seems to have changed overnight. They have disowned a thing which they agreed was suitable to begin with. I hope that is nothing more than coincidence.
Thank you for the compliment.

Never during the course of the negotiations did the Newfoundland government once suggest the amount was too small. I admit it is small, because it is approximately 35 per cent of the total drop of income of the Newfoundland fishermen in 1961 as compared with I960. The hon. member has contrasted this amount of $300,000 with the $42 million paid as an acreage

Supply-Fisheries
payment to the western farmers. I say that this $300,000 is 35 per cent of the loss of income in the one year as compared with the other to the Newfoundland fishermen. Well, the $42 million just approved by this committee represents only 10 per cent of the drop in income experienced by the western farmers from one year to the next.
Since I have become minister in charge of this department I have taken a special interest in the fishermen of Newfoundland. It has been suggested by hon. members from the west coast that my interest is too great. I make no apologies, because Newfoundland, as far as government services are concerned, has a great deal of catching up to do. It is my intention to do what I can to improve the situation in which the fishermen of Newfoundland make their living. It is a hard life. Since I have been minister my department has doubled the outlets for subsidized bait to Newfoundland. We have increased the subsidy on long-liners and larger vessels of that sort in order that the fishermen may go out and fish where the fish are to be found rather than be dependant on the fish coming close to shore. There are many other things I could say. My department is most anxious to do what it can for the fishermen of Newfoundland so as to improve their lot, and I am not going to sell them short. I have a great deal of respect for the fishermen of Newfoundland. I know them to be a selfreliant, hardworking, honourable class of people.
Having said that, I want to say, in closing, only this: I do not pretend that this is the whole answer to all the ills of the fishermen of Newfoundland or that in the administration and distribution of this grant there will not be some who will feel they should have got more or that others are getting too much. There are bound to be difficulties and criticisms. Has there ever been anyone who has fried to improve the lot of his fellowmen who has not been criticized? The hon member for Bonavista-Twillingate has taken 50 minutes to express his point of view. I see it is ten o'clock, now, and I am going to sit down, but the hon. member has taken 50 minutes to pour scorn on this item and all I can say is that if I thought an item was as bad as this one is in his opinion I would not want to be associated with it. So I invite the hon. member who, I presume, is speaking for his
party, to get up and move that this item be reduced to $1 if he feels that way about it.

speechtext:
Shall vote 612
carry?
Carried.

Item agreed to.
Resolutions adopted in committee of supply this day reported and concurred in.
Before we adjourn perhaps the house leader could indicate what we will do for the rest of the week. It would be of help if he could do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: We will continue with the program I outlined yesterday, namely conclude the supplementary estimates and then go on with the resolutions standing in the name of the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
If that business is completed tomorrow, can the minister say whether we would resume on Thursday debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The type of question that is offered to me is one that I could answer if the members of the opposition would tell me when we are going to complete the business that I have already outlined.
It being three minutes after ten o'clock
the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.

Production and marketing branch-
611.	Payments to western grain producers to be distributed on the following basis, namely, $1 per cultivated acre up to a maximum of 200 acres per farm in accordance with regulations of the governor in council, $42,000,000.

Special-
612.	Contribution towards a special Newfoundland works program for fishing settlements that experienced income reduction resulting from decreased catches, $300,000.
